#4448. Drive with Style: Our Favorite Chronographs & Driving Watches (Mostly) under $1000

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether you’re buying a gift for a car lover or just looking to step up your style, check out our favorite watches and chronographs for drivers.

This story was updated in November 2026 with new products and fresh information.

As a watch enthusiast, I know all too well the dilemma friends, partners, and family members face when trying to buy a watch as a gift. Watch people can be incredibly particular. We obsess over case sizes, movements, bracelet designs, dial layouts, and brand history in the same way car enthusiasts argue over engine codes or wheel specs.

That’s what makes this list different. These aren’t cheap knockoffs or forgettable department-store watches. Instead, they’re enthusiast-focused timepieces that capture the spirit, heritage, and personality that make great watches special, without requiring luxury-watch money.

I’ve rounded up a nice selection of vintage-inspired chronographs, quirky design icons, and motorsport-influenced watches that genuine enthusiasts will appreciate, wear often, and happily give real wrist time to long after the wrapping paper is gone.

The Timex Atelier Chronograph Quartz M1q brings a more considered design approach to an accessible everyday chronograph. Its balanced 40mm stainless-steel case, refined subdial layout, and engraved black dial give it a premium look without feeling overly busy, while a double-curved sapphire crystal adds a welcome touch of durability. A Swiss-made quartz chronograph movement keeps time accurately, without the added cost or maintenance of an automatic, and the tachymeter scale offers a useful nod to traditional motorsport watches. It’s available with either an oil- and chemical-resistant NBR rubber strap or a self-adjusting stainless-steel bracelet, and its 100-meter water resistance makes it practical beyond the watch box.

The PRS 516 features a 42mm case, perforated leather strap, and piston-inspired pushers, all nodding directly to Sixties motorsport, while the Swiss automatic chronograph movement underneath gives it legitimate credibility. Tissot has been tied to racing for decades, and the PRS 516 leans into that heritage without feeling like a costume piece. It’s sporty, tactile, and busy in the best possible way.

The Timex Marlin Neo Classic Chronograph takes one of the brand’s most recognizable vintage designs and gives it a cleaner, more streamlined look. Its compact 40mm brushed stainless-steel case, polished top ring, and curved pushers preserve the Marlin’s mid-century character, while three dial and strap combinations offer slightly different takes on the same retro-inspired design. Details like the domed acrylic crystal, multiscale dial markings, and tachymeter scale give it the feel of a vintage instrument watch without making it overly busy. Inside, a quartz chronograph movement provides accurate, low-maintenance timekeeping and a functional stopwatch, making the Neo Classic a handsome everyday option for anyone drawn to classic watch design.

The Form C feels like the automotive equivalent of a stripped-down Bauhaus sports coupe: clean, lightweight, and engineered with restraint. Its 40mm stainless-steel case wears slim, thanks to Junghans’s minimalist German design language, while the calfskin leather strap keeps things understated and comfortable. A reliable quartz chronograph movement fits the watch’s no-nonsense personality and gives it dead-simple usability. Junghans’s heritage stretches back to 1861, and the Form C channels that legacy into a watch that’s more about precision and proportion than flash.

The Seiko Prospex Speedtimer SSC947 pairs motorsport heritage with modern tech in a 41.4 mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished finishing. Powered by Seiko’s solar V192 movement, it offers a chronograph, 24-hour subdial, power-reserve indicator, and date display, with a six-month reserve when fully charged. The 947 model is my favorite version of the Speedtimer, with its awesome yellow dial. Protected by a curved sapphire crystal with inner antireflective coating and mounted on a three-link stainless bracelet, it’s water-resistant to 100 meters. Seiko’s reputation as a favorite among horologists speaks to the brand’s consistent quality, innovation, and mechanical mastery, making the SSC947 a reliable and stylish choice for both collectors and racing enthusiasts alike.

If the yellow dial is a bit too bold, you can also check out the SSC943 in Ivory and Green, and the panda-dialed SSC813.

Nicknamed the “Bullhead,” the Tsuno Chronograph wears its motorsport inspiration proudly, with its pushers mounted at the top of the 45mm case like vintage rally timers. Citizen revived the design from the brand’s iconic Seventies Bullhead chronographs, combining retro styling with modern Eco-Drive solar-powered quartz tech that eliminates battery changes. It’s bold, unapologetically funky, and one of the most distinctive modern chronographs you can buy without crossing into luxury-watch pricing.

Featuring a 41mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished surfaces, this Alpina Startimer is powered by a quartz chronograph movement. A large “Big Date” window sits at 6 o’clock, and a 100-meter water-resistance rating ensures a bit of water won’t be a worry. The white dial sports bold numerals, luminous hands, and a red-triangle chronograph seconds hand, and it is protected by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal. It comes with a three-link stainless-steel bracelet and delivers chronograph utility in a clean, sporty package.

The Conquest Chronograph features a 42mm stainless-steel case, ceramic tachymeter bezel, and automatic chronograph movement, striking an excellent balance between luxury and sportiness. Longines has deep roots in timing motorsport and aviation events dating back over a century, and the Conquest channels that pedigree into a polished, well-rounded package.

The Bulova Racer 150th Anniversary Shelby pairs motorsport style with serious precision. Powered by Precisionist movement, it delivers exceptional accuracy and a smooth sweeping second hand, plus a 1/1000-second chronograph for track-ready performance. The bold blue dial, sapphire crystal, and 43mm stainless-steel case channel classic racing design, while the lightweight striped rubber strap keeps it comfortable for everyday wear. Rugged, refined, and collector-worthy, this limited-edition timepiece is engineered to stand out.

The Bulova Racer Chronograph stands out thanks to its sharp case lines, bold subdials, and an aggressive motorsport-inspired aesthetic. Its stainless-steel case measures around 42mm and pairs with a sporty bracelet setup, while the quartz chronograph movement emphasizes precision and practicality. Bulova’s long history in American watchmaking, including timing innovations and racing partnerships, gives the Racer more authenticity than its flashy styling initially suggests.

The Legacy Tonneau Chronograph has a distinctly Seventies flavor, with its curved rectangular case shape and integrated-bracelet-inspired design evoking vintage sports watches of the era. Timex keeps things simple with a quartz chronograph movement and stainless-steel construction that prioritizes durability and affordability over pretense. The tonneau-shaped case wears differently from traditional round chronographs, giving it a cool retro personality. It’s proof that enthusiast-oriented design doesn’t have to come with a luxury-watch price tag

The Citizen Eco-Drive Weekender Brycen Chronograph is a sharp, 44 mm watch with a bold blue dial that looks great on the wrist. It’s powered by light, so you never need to change a battery, and it packs a chronograph, 12/24‑hour time, a date window, and 100-meter water resistance. Stylish, tough, and low-maintenance, it’s perfect for everyday wear or weekend adventures.

The Ventura Chrono is pure mid-century Americana. Its asymmetrical 32.3mm-by-50.3mm triangular case design became iconic after Elvis Presley famously wore one, and Hamilton has kept the look alive with modern chronograph hardware and a supple leather strap. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, the Ventura trades traditional racing-watch cues for style and wrist presence. It’s like a Sixties concept car brought to life.

The Swatch New Chrono takes a lighthearted approach to a chronograph, with a 43mm stainless‑steel case, intuitive chronograph subdials, a tachymeter bezel, and a reliable Swiss quartz movement. Whether you’re timing sprint starts or simply want a watch that looks dynamic on your wrist, this piece combines accessible build quality, youthful design cues, and a distinctive racing-inspired spirit.

This iconic watch retains the classic Marlin Sixties design features that make it so cool and timeless. With a domed acrylic crystal lens and retro-style square markers at 3, 9, and 12 o'clock, it features a natural leather strap and a tachymeter index along its outer minute track to measure speed. We dig the racing stripes on this blue version, but many face and band combinations are available.

Built for serious outdoor missions, this timepiece features a rugged 45mm Carbonox case, unidirectional bezel, and 300-meter water resistance, ready for land, sea, or whatever the trail throws at you. With 18 tritium light tubes that ensure visibility for up to 25 years, an orange screw-in crown, and the “Never Give Up” motto engraved on the caseback alongside Bear Grylls’s signature, it combines Swiss precision with no-compromise practicality.

Featuring a distinctive square resin case, the AE1200WHD‑1A is a retro‑futuristic digital watch built for function and value. It offers world time across 31 time zones (48 cities + UTC), a 1/100‑second stopwatch, a countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full auto‑calendar up to 2099. With an impressively long 10‑year battery life, 100-meter water resistance, LED backlight, and a stainless‑steel bracelet, it is the perfect beater watch for a seasoned horologist or a gateway drug to the uninitiated.

The Timex Q Chronograph blends vintage charm with modern functionality in a stainless-steel 38mm case that channels late-Seventies sports-watch aesthetics. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it features a day-date window, a rotating bezel, and subtle retro accents such as a distressed leather strap.

#4447. Audi Has Officially Ended Production of the A8 Flagship Sedan

After more than thirty years, Audi presses pause on its biggest sedan.

Ever since Skipp Sudduth asked for “Something very Fast. Audi S8. Something that can shove a little bit,” in 1998's Ronin, Audi's big body sedan has been the stuff of legend. Mercedes-Benz S-Class? Too obvious. BMW 7-Series? You don't want to look like a wannabe James Bond. But an Audi A8? That's what you drive when you have a nickname like The Transporter.

However, as appealing as the A8 is on-screen, it's not really been much of a mover in Audi showrooms of late. Almost nothing depreciates faster than a full-size German luxury sedan—you might as well invest in an ice sculpture—and both BMW and Mercedes have been outselling Audi in the segment. Thus, Audi has just pressed pause on production of the A8, with no immediate plans in place to reboot it.

See all results for new 2027 Audi A8 for sale near 32763

The Neckarsulm plant where the A8 was being built has already pivoted to production of the Audi A5 in both sedan and Avant forms, in standard and S5 or RS5 trims. Audi has been headquartered in Ingolstadt since the 1980s, long enough to have that city be shorthand for the company the way Stuttgart is for Porsche, but the Neckarsulm plant has roots stretching back to the nineteenth century via NSU, one of the companies that ended up forming Audi's four rings

Launched in 1994, the A8 arrived with aluminum-intensive construction to keep weight down and an available 4.2-liter V8 that still rates as one of the best-sounding engines ever made. It was businesslike, composed with all-wheel-drive for all conditions, managing to be both discreet and muscular, like a bodyguard in a well-tailored suit.

Subsequent generations remained a little more understated than rivals from Mercedes and BMW, but the fifth-gen car that's just exited production was only a year away from celebrating its tenth birthday. Even with a mid-cycle facelift, that's a bit long in the tooth for a flagship.

Taking over flagship duties is Audi's Q9 SUV, a proper three-row family hauler that's aimed at the BMW X7 and Mercedes GLS. The Q9 is certainly large and imposing, and it can carry more passengers and cargo than any A8 model. Does it have that same charisma? Put it this way: Jason Bateman is a very talented actor and producer. He is not Jason Statham.

Meanwhile, Audi may return with some kind of electrified successor to the A8, perhaps as an extended, embiggened version of whatever the new battery-electric A4 ends up looking like. Until then, any Audi-loving underworld soldiers of fortune will have to make do with a brown Mercedes 450 SEL 6.9 and a rocket launcher.

#4446. This New EV Motor Spins At 30,000 RPM. Here's Why That Matters

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

An electric motor spinning at 30,000 rpm sounds like something you might find in a high-power EV supercar. ZF has something less extravagant in mind: making the hardware that powers everyday EVs smaller, lighter, and less hungry for expensive materials.

ZF’s new High Revolution Drive combines the motor, power electronics, and transmission all in the same housing. Unlike Mercedes-Benz, though, it doesn't also put the brakes inside the same housing.

Compared with one of ZF’s comparable Select drive units, which spins up to 18,000 rpm, the company claims nearly 25% less weight and volume, half the magnet mass, and a similar efficiency of almost 93%.

This helps because less mass improves EV range, and fewer magnets reduce costs and supply-chain dependence.

According to ZF, spinning the motor faster lets it deliver the same power from a smaller, lighter package. Gears then reduce that speed and increase the turning force sent to the wheels, using a reduction ratio of about 18:1. The version ZF showed produces up to 268 horsepower, with the gearing delivering peak torque of 2,581 pound-feet (3,500 Nm) to the wheels.

The torque measurement comes after the gearing has multiplied the motor’s output. The “two-stage transmission” doesn’t actually mean a two-speed gearbox. It describes successive gear reductions, not two separate driving ratios.

The company says the production High Revolution Drive should deliver 200 to 268 hp and work with both 400- and 800-volt platforms. Reusing its modular Select architecture should simplify installation, shorten development and control costs, and retain manufacturing flexibility. Talks with automakers are underway, with production targeted by 2030.

ZF isn’t alone in trying to squeeze more useful output from a smaller package. One prototype of Yasa’s ultra-compact axial-flux motor produced over 1,000 hp and weighed just 28 pounds. That’s its short-term peak figure, with continuous output estimated at 469–536 bhp.

Yasa’s figure describes only the motor, while ZF’s weight reduction refers to the whole integrated drive unit. Gearing and power electronics still need somewhere to live, and they also add weight.

ZF has also introduced repair kits intended to let workshops fix individual drive unit components, such as gearbox bearings, instead of replacing entire assemblies. That addresses a different problem from shrinking and making hardware lighter, but one buyers may care about considerably more once the warranty expires.

However, ZF hasn’t said whether these two developments are connected, or whether the kits it revealed should be taken as a repairability promise for this new drive. There’s also no mention of which production EV would get this new drive unit. We also don’t know whether those engineering gains will remain unchanged from today’s announcement to something you can actually buy.

Still, this kind of EV development deserves attention even without a four-figure horsepower claim. A family car doesn’t need to break acceleration records, but making its drive unit lighter and less expensive (and possibly easier to repair, too) is exactly what it needs. Whether any savings reach buyers is another question, but giving cars the same power with smaller and less hardware is a good place to start.

#4445. Lucid says service wait times fell 20% after 40% jump in service staff

Lucid (LCID) says service wait times dropped 20% globally in the third quarter after it grew its technician and service-support staff by more than 40% in a single quarter.

The automaker is also adding Studio and Service Centers in Southern California, Los Angeles, Dallas, and the Chicago suburbs, plus 20 more Gravity Mobile Service vans. It’s a clear sign that service had become a problem for Lucid owners.

Lucid announced the numbers today, a day after its Q3 2026 earnings. Both comparisons are against the second quarter, not a year ago.

The hiring isn’t done either. After a 40%-plus increase in technicians, advisors, and concierges in Q3, Lucid wants that figure at 50% by the end of 2026 and 60% by Q1 2027. Mobile Service capacity in North America grew 15%, with a 40% target for year-end.

That’s a big hiring push for a company that laid off 18% of its workforce in June, its second cut in four months after a 12% reduction in February. Roughly 1,500 people left across those two rounds.

And owners noticed. On the LucidOwners forum, one Air Touring owner posted in early October that Lucid told them in writing to expect “a service time of about 7 weeks” at its Beverly Hills Service Center. Other threads blamed service-department layoffs for slow repairs and recall work.

Billy Hayes, Lucid’s Chief Customer Officer, said the company is “adding service personnel, and increasing Mobile Service capacity to reduce wait times and provide more convenient, responsive support.”

Here’s what’s opening, according to Lucid:

Lucid is also letting a growing number of its Certified Collision shops handle recall campaign work, which should take some pressure off its own Service Centers.

Outside the US, the expansion leans on partners. Munsterhuis Autobedrijven is Lucid’s first retail partner in the Netherlands (Hengelo), Cloppenburg Automobil SE opens a Duisburg retail and service site in January 2027, Autohaus Possögel starts authorized service in Naumburg, Germany, in December, and Emil Frey France will support Lucid’s launch in France. In Saudi Arabia, Lucid opened its first company-owned Body & Paint Repair Center in Riyadh, with more service sites in Riyadh and Dammam coming in the first half of 2027.

Lucid doesn’t say what the average wait time actually is.

A 20% drop from seven weeks is still more than five weeks. A 20% drop from one week is a non-issue. Without a baseline, owners can’t tell which one they’re getting.

It’s also hard to separate better service from fewer cars coming in. Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while it worked through inventory. Its fleet keeps growing, but slowly.

For context, Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3, five times Lucid’s volume, and it’s been leaning hard on mobile service too. Lucid is a much smaller operation trying to cover the US, Europe, and the Middle East with a thin network.

This is the right move, and it’s overdue.

Lucid has been one of the few EV startups with genuinely class-leading hardware. The Air’s efficiency is still unmatched and the Gravity is a great vehicle on paper, even if we found its software wasn’t ready. But when you’re asking someone to spend $80,000 or more on a car from a brand with an uncertain future, the ownership experience is half the sale. A seven-week wait for a repair kills that sale, and the referrals that come after it.

So growing service staff by 40% in a quarter is a big deal. It also tells you how thin those teams had gotten after two rounds of layoffs. Lucid cut too deep in the wrong place, and it’s now hiring to fix it.

The problem is the timing and the money. Lucid burned $1.04 billion in free cash flow in Q3 and only stays funded into late 2027 because the PIF just added another $1.75 billion. Meanwhile, the Midsize “Cosmos” that’s supposed to bring real volume doesn’t start production until the second half of 2027. Service is exactly where Lucid should spend between now and then, because the buyers it has today are the ones who’ll decide whether anybody trusts the brand with a cheaper EV.

#4444. 10,000 Miles with Our 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450, and the Love Bombing Continues

We can’t get enough of the way the E-class drives.

If you were friends with our long-term Mercedes-Benz E450, and it was in a relationship with someone like us, you’d be no doubt cautioning your friend about our love bombing. The logbook is stuffed, page after page, with over-the-top praise. Here’s a smattering of some recent musings: “Arguably the most comfortable long-termer we’ve ever had,” says managing news editor Eric Stafford. Senior news editor Caleb Miller added, “The E450 just feels so effortless and relaxing that I feel like I could drive across the country in one day in this thing.” And Miller also gave a shoutout to the 21-speaker Burmester sound system. Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga, who is known to sign out the E-class for extended chunks of time, adds, “Makes you feel so relaxed when you drive it—supple ride, glorious seats, rich interior, plus summer-tire grip.” But Buyer’s Guide director Rich Ceppos may have bestowed the highest praise: “Of the 500-plus models we cover, if I had to pick one car to live with and drive every day, it’d be this one.”

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 37923

It’s safe to say we’re smitten with the way the E-class drives, an ideal blend of comfort and liveliness. If we had one nit to pick it would be the slight impact harshness from the 20-inch wheels and tires and their relatively shallow sidewalls. We’d probably like the ride better with the base 18-inch wheel-and-tire package and its additional sidewall, although it’s a major visual downgrade.

The E450 drives so well, and its 375-hp turbo inline-six is so smooth and melodious, that we’d be more than willing to overlook so-so fuel economy. But the E-class continues to impress there, too, with an overall average of 27 mpg, one better than its EPA combined figure. And that’s with a lot of heavy-footed commuting and not all that many road trips. On longer drives, we’ve seen mpg numbers in the high 30s.

Fall’s cooler temperatures have us in a warm glow about the E450’s not only heated steering wheel and seats (both pretty common nowadays) but also the heated center and outboard armrests, part of the $2950 Multicontour Seating package—decadent, perhaps, but a lovely way to start your commute on a chilly morning.

Our primary complaints tend to be about anything but the driving, including the touch-sensitive controls on the steering wheel, the door handles that sometimes don’t power out of the body quick enough, or the fingerprint-prone piano-black interior trim and vast array of three screens across the interior. We’ve also gotten plenty cross with the virtual assistant, which chimes in with obnoxious frequency if left to its automatic setting, interrupting conversations about everything from building developments in the area to the price of an item discussed. We quickly switched it back to having to hear the “Hey, Mercedes” wake phrase before inserting itself.

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 37923

You know the honeymoon phase is waning when it comes time to start paying for maintenance. Mercedes specifies service for the E-class every 10,000 miles or 12 months, with the first one a simple oil change and various inspections. We felt the Mercedes markup paying that $478 bill, and our local dealer added another $62 of oil and fuel additives that aren’t called for in the owner’s manual and without asking our approval (we’ve excluded this charge from the service-cost tally).

The only other pause in the enjoyment of our E450 was when a screw found its way into the right-front tire in a spot where it couldn’t be plugged. So, we had to shell out $420 for a new tire from Tire Rack, which was there the next day.

Can the love last? We have another 30,000 miles to find out.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 11,134 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 27 mpgFuel Tank Size: 17.4 gal Observed Fuel Range: 460 milesService: $478 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0Damage and Destruction: $420

Ever since this long-term 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450 arrived, it has served us daily reminders why we named this excellent luxury sedan to our 10Best list for two years running. Some of that luxury comes from the fact that we could not drive the car in any other way, because it showed up with a mere 20 miles on its odometer and we were driving gently to follow the 1000-mile break-in requirements. Either way, its ride refinement and all-around sophistication have received continuous accolades since day one. Everyone in the office is already gushing over the E-class's ride quality, refinement, and seat comfort.

Of course, once we hit the 1000-mile mark, we picked up the pace. The around-town ride feels almost floaty, so you'd think that hurling it down a back road would take the E450 out of its element, but it remains tied down and settled no matter how hard you push. Skidpad grip of 0.92 g is excellent for the class, as is braking from 70 mph in 157 feet, which is an identical result to the last BMW M5 we tested.

The E450's inline-six, which pairs exclusively with all-wheel drive and is a $5900 upgrade over the four-cylinder-powered E350, is not only smooth and sonorous, but also extraordinarily fuel efficient. We measured a whopping 39 mpg in our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, which is 6 mpg better than its EPA highway figure. Combined with a decently sized 17.4-gallon fuel tank, that means our E-class can make it nearly 700 miles on a single fill-up. The E450 returns excellent fuel economy beyond purposefully gentle driving too; our current running average of 27 mpg is 1 mpg higher than its EPA combined rating. Considering the straight-line hustle the 375-hp six commands—60 mph in a brisk 4.5 seconds and the quarter-mile in 12.9 seconds—that fuel economy is seriously impressive.

But the steering wheel's touch-sensitive controls are despised as much as the car's overall driving demeanor is loved. Everything from the volume control to the cruise set speed requires a swipe on the steering-wheel spokes, which sometimes does nothing, sometimes provides more adjustment than you're looking for, and rarely does exactly what you want.

Our long-term E450 is packed full of options, taking the price up to $95,375 from its $73,650 starting point. There are a few things that the majority of us could do without, including the front passenger screen and selfie camera (part of the $1500 Superscreen package) and the $990 3-D gauge cluster display. But the $3400 Pinnacle trim, which includes a thumpin' 21-speaker Burmester stereo, and the $3200 air springs that bolster ride quality are outlays that we'd spend our own money on. We also thought ahead to winter; tucked into the various option packages are heaters for the front armrests, steering wheel, rear seats, and washer nozzles. There's really only one feature that we wish we had, and that's soft-close doors, which cost an additional $550. We're fans of the Verde Silver Metallic green paint, and the $1950 20-inch AMG multi-spoke wheels are a serious visual upgrade over the base 18s.

The E-class is not at all ostentatious, but it still gets noticed, with many a parking-lot bystander lobbing praise in the E-class's direction. We agree, it's a fantastic luxury sedan, and we look forward to spending a lot more time driving it to see if we're as smitten with the ownership experience.

#4443. Toyota Tundra Driver Hits 130 MPH in Police Chase, Then Claims He Was Asleep in the Back Seat: Cops

Police say the driver jumped in the back while the truck was spinning after a PIT maneuver, then tried to convince them he had nothing to do with the chase.

Police officers have heard all sorts of excuses from speeders, from trying to get to work on time to running late for a haircut. Chances are, whatever excuse you try, the police have heard it before. That said, a Toyota Tundra driver that police say recently lead them on a 130-mile-per-hour chase in Florida may have tried the most unique excuse ever: according to Gulf Coast News, the man claimed he was sleeping in the back seat the whole time.

WINK News reports that a Collier County Sheriff's Office Corporal saw a beige Toyota Tundra at about 2:20 a.m. running over a curb while attempting to get to a gas station in Naples, Florida. The Toyota reportedly refused to stop for police; a chase ensued, and authorities claim the truck hit speeds of 130 mph in 45-mile-per-hour zones—impressive velocity, for a Tundra. Deputies reportedly deployed stop sticks, successfully puncturing the Tundra's tires, but that still didn’t end the chase; authorities say it took a PIT maneuver to finally bring the truck to a halt.

Then, it seems, things took an odd turn. According to the arrest report, a passenger told deputies that the driver, identified as Oswaldo Perez-Ramirez, jumped from the driver's seat into the back seat—while the truck was spinning after the PIT maneuver. When officers questioned Perez-Ramirez, he reportedly insisted he hadn't been driving at all; in fact, he allegedly claimed he'd been sleeping in the back seat.

However, that story fell apart when police reviewed the dashcam video, and it showed the driver wearing a white shirt; Perez-Ramirez was also wearing a white shirt when officers removed him from the truck, police say. He was subsequently arrested and faces charges of fleeing and eluding, fleeing and eluding at a high rate of speed, driving without a valid license, failure to stop, and DUI.

#4442. Ford's Radical New EV Manufacturing Process Is Already Building Trucks

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

During its recent quarterly earnings call, one Ford executive revealed that it has already begun rolling Fathoms off the line at its recently revamped factory in Louisville well ahead of the affordable electric pickup's late-2027 delivery schedule.

"It's progressing very well," said Ford COO, Kumar Galhotra, during the company's recent quarterly earnings call. "90% of the validation testing has been completed. We've built our first production line vehicles at Louisville assembly plant."

Importantly, Galhotra didn't say these are production vehicles. Rather, these are the first Fathoms built on their real production line. Essentially, these validation vehicles are the beginning of Ford proving out its production process for both the Fathom and its Universal Electric Vehicle Platform. It's an important milestone for Ford, which has bet its electric future on the UEV platform and a radically different method of manufacturing cars than it's used before.

Ford will build the Fathom using a so-called "assembly tree" rather than the assembly line Henry Ford pioneered a century ago. The front, middle, and rear sections of the pickup will be put together simultaneously, then joined together toward the end of the process. Ford says this should allow it to build vehicles quicker and more efficiently, in part by making the ergonomics better for its workers. It resembles the "unboxed" process Tesla has introduced for the Cybercab.

Ford has been building cars for more than a century, but a new EV on a new platform using new manufacturing techniques needs to be fleshed out—especially if Ford wants to quickly hit the production volumes it's reportedly targeting: 100,000 sales in the first year. As Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in the midst of the company's period of production hell: "It's relatively easy to make a prototype, but extremely difficult to mass manufacture a vehicle reliably at scale."

The testing isn't just limited to the Louisville plant where more than $2 billion was invested to manufacture the Fathom. Ford's Shelbyville Technical Center has also been cranking out large castings used to underpin its affordable electric pickup.

These large castings are made in a similar way to Tesla's Gigacasting process with the goal being to cut down on the production complexity (and cost) of the Fathom. In total, it takes 146 different parts into just 2 large castings. Galhotra says that Ford has already made 5,000 of these unicastings and has effectively substantiated its ability to build this new tech at a high rate.

The next challenge, according to the COO, is the rest of the supply chain:

"We need to make sure that the supply base can run at rate with high quality parts," said Galhotra "And that's very normal at this stage of the launch, and that's what we're going to be working on for the next few months."

The Blue Oval doesn't plan on delivering any of these pickups for about a year, which means that it still has time to ramp things up and make sure the so-called "assembly tree" is running smoothly. The Fathom could prove out to be Ford's EV redemption arc if the automaker gets it right. Affordable? Check. Versatile? Check. Scalable? That's to be seen.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis said the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

The GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

#4439. Lotus’s New V-8 Ferrari Fighter Is Coming in 2028; Here’s the Engine That Will Power It

Horse Powertrains has pulled the wraps off its first eight-cylinder powerplant, destined for the Lotus Type 135.

Back in May, Lotus revealed its Focus 2030 strategy for the future, in which the storied British racing and sports car brand aims to return to its roots by “protecting what makes Lotus, Lotus.” What makes Lotus Lotus is, of course, at least partially combustion-powered performance cars that follow Colin Chapman’s maxim to “simplify and add lightness.” As a thrilling nod in that direction, Lotus confirmed plans to launch its first supercar, the Type 135—which may become the new Esprit.

Now, we now know what will power it. On Tuesday, Horse Powertrain—a Geely subsidiary alongside Lotus—unveiled its new Horse W40 powerplant, which the company has confirmed the will power the Lotus Type 135. Horse also manufactures the new V-6 engine that will replace the supercharged Toyota V-6 in the Emira sports car.

The Horse W40 is a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 with a hot-vee configuration, designed for use in high-performance hybrid vehicle platforms. It weighs just 441 pounds, but it can produce an impressive peak output of over 670 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque all on its own. When paired with a hybrid component, Lotus said the Type 135 will be able to deliver more than 986 hp.

The Horse W40 uses a proprietary 8LDCT transmission. It’s an eight-speed transmission with a “sportscar-grade wet dual clutch.” Horse Powertrain claims a shift response time of less than 20 milliseconds, and the transmission can handle up to 774 pound-feet of torque.

Lotus has not yet provided full details about the Type 135—those will be announced before the end of 2026—but the company has confirmed it plans to launch the new machine in 2028. The Type 135 will be all-new, distinct from the Emira; Lotus expects to build the supercar in Europe, unlike the China-made Eletre and Emeya EVs, which may reduce the potential exposure to American tariffs. Lotus has revealed a teaser image of the new car, showing a dual exhaust and a large diffuser.

The Lotus Type 135 may not be the only application for this engine, either. Horse Powertrain says the engine’s low-end torque could be used for trucks and off-road vehicles, if you’ve been keeping a candle lit for Geely-owned Volvo to build a raucous but Scandinavian minimalist Mercedes G-Wagen competitor. (Hey, everyone else seems to be doing it...)

#4438. Unit1 FARO and NEON review: I just found my new favorite e-bike helmets

I test a lot of electric bikes, which means I also spend a lot of time wearing bicycle helmets. And while most helmets tend to fall into the decidedly unexciting category of “necessary safety equipment,” UNIT 1 has managed to make a couple that I actually get excited about wearing.

I’ve been using both the UNIT 1 FARO and the new NEON, and despite taking fairly different approaches, they’ve both become regular go-to helmets for me.

The FARO is the more futuristic-looking of the two, and it’s also the one that really leans into the “smart helmet” concept.

The helmet includes MIPS protection to reduce rotational impact during a collision, as well as integrated lighting on both the front and rear, including a large customizable rear lighting area made up of dozens of LEDs.

That large rear LED array is a feature I particularly appreciate since visibility is such a major part of cycling safety.

A helmet obviously can’t force drivers to pay attention, but I’d rather give them as many opportunities as possible to see me. The hidden light area below the obvious LED light bar adds a lot of extra visibility.

You can see just how vivid it is in the GIF below, though in real life it looks even better!

The FARO’s lighting system works with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote, which adds turn signals controlled right from the bars.

The system can also provide automatic brake-light functionality, giving you another way to communicate with traffic around you.

I’ll admit that turn signals on bicycles can sometimes feel a bit gimmicky, especially when they’re so close together that drivers can’t really tell which direction is flashing. But putting them high up on the helmet makes them considerably more visible, and the little wireless handlebar remote makes operating them incredibly easy.

The rechargeable lighting is also convenient. I’ve topped up the helmet from a power bank while out and about, meaning you don’t necessarily need to find a wall outlet if you realize your helmet is running low. The rear LED light bar also turns green and illuminates along the length of the bar to let you know what percentage of charge the battery has reached. The only way it could be clearer would be with a screen, but we’re still talking about a helmet here, not a phone.

There are other smart features packed in too, including crash detection and app-based customization.

The tradeoff is weight. At around 640 grams for a medium, the FARO is noticeably heavier than a conventional bicycle helmet. It doesn’t bother me much once I’m riding, and I’ve found the helmet comfortable, but you definitely know there’s more helmet up there. Each time I pick it up, I’m reminded that it’s not just the basic little foam shell that I’ve been wearing for the last few years.

Then there’s the price. At around $230 (or $195 during the current Black Friday sale period), this isn’t a cheap helmet. You’re paying for all of that technology, lighting, and design.

As much as I like the FARO, I’ve also become a big fan of the UNIT 1 NEON.

At roughly 430 grams in a medium, it’s significantly lighter than the FARO, and that difference is immediately noticeable. It’s also a bit cheaper at around $210 (or $178 during the Black Friday sale period) while still packing several of the smart features that make UNIT 1’s helmets interesting.

You still get MIPS rotational protection, crash detection, integrated rear lighting, app connectivity, and compatibility with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote for turn signals and brake-light functionality.

I do wish the NEON had a front light like the FARO. That’s probably the biggest feature I miss when switching between the two. But the NEON makes up for it with one of my favorite features on either helmet: its magnetic face shield.

The shield is ridiculously easy to attach and remove. You don’t even need to carefully line it up. I just need to get it somewhere near the mounting points with one hand and the powerful magnets basically grab it out of the air and snap it into position.

That means I can easily add or remove it one-handed, even while riding.

The photochromic shield is clear enough for night riding but darkens when exposed to bright sunlight, giving you sun protection without requiring separate daytime and nighttime shields. I’ve found that incredibly convenient, especially on rides that transition from daylight into evening. I hate that I can’t wear my sunglasses for eye protection at night, and a lens like this solves that issue.

The NEON also gets something particularly important for faster e-bike riders: NTA 8776 certification. That’s the Dutch standard designed specifically around higher-speed e-bike uses at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). For the Class 3 e-bikes that have become increasingly common in the US, that’s a big distinction compared to helmets rated for crashes at slower speeds.

That’s actually difficult, because I regularly use both.

The FARO is the one I’d choose if maximum visibility and technology were my priorities. I love having LEDs both front and rear, the MIPS protection, and the handlebar-controlled turn signals. It’s comfortable, looks great, and has become one of my favorite urban riding helmets.

But the NEON may be the easier helmet to recommend to most e-bike riders.

It’s lighter, a little cheaper, still gives you a rear light and smart safety features, has that excellent magnetic photochromic face shield, and importantly carries NTA 8776 certification for faster e-bike riding.

Neither helmet is inexpensive, and the FARO in particular asks you to accept some extra weight in exchange for all that technology. But I’m used to wearing much heavier motorcycle helmets and ways.

Plus, it’s important to note that these aren’t helmets I tested for a few rides and then tossed onto a shelf. Both have stayed in my regular rotation, and I find myself reaching for them frequently when I head out on an e-bike. The fact that I not only enjoyed them during my testing but actually replaced my old helmets with them should speak for itself.

For someone who rides as much as I do, that’s probably the strongest endorsement I can give them.

Between solid helmets like these and safe riding clothing, it’s good to feel protected!

#4437. BMW Is Embracing Cheaper LFP Batteries For Its Newest EVs

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Between the 435-mile iX3 and 468-mile i3, BMW’s newest EVs make a strong case for spending a bit more to get incredible range. Now the company is looking at accommodating buyers who don’t need that much range and would rather keep some extra money in their pockets.

Speaking during BMW’s third-quarter earnings call, CEO Milan Nedeljkovic confirmed that the company will expand its use of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for Neue Klasse EVs, potentially opening the door to more affordable electric BMWs. BMW considers the cylindrical nickel-manganese-cobalt cells that are in most Neue Klasse cars as superior for the range they deliver, he said, but he acknowledged that LFP offers a different balance of cost and range.

“We will add the LFP technology in our vehicles, but we will be very specific in which vehicle and for which purpose,” Nedeljkovic said without naming the next models getting it or specifying a launch date outside China. Nor did he promise that lower battery costs would translate directly into lower sticker prices.

China already offers a preview of the strategy. The entry-level, long-wheelbase iX3 30L uses a 77-kilowatt-hour LFP battery, while the more expensive 40L and 50L have NMC packs. The 30L has a claimed CLTC range of 630 kilometers (391 miles), although the Chinese test cycle is more optimistic than WLTP and EPA.

LFP's cost advantage starts with what goes into it. The cathode it uses is relatively inexpensive iron and phosphate instead of the nickel and cobalt found in NMC cells. It’s also known to generally offer high longevity, thermal stability, and less degradation from frequent fast charging to 100%. The catch is lower energy density, which makes NMC more attractive, especially for longer-range applications.

BMW could introduce LFP versions of existing models, following the Chinese iX3’s example. Its forthcoming smaller Neue Klasse EV also looks like a strong candidate for LFP. BMW has confirmed a compact Euro-focused electric model is coming in 2028, bringing its new technology into a more affordable segment.

Choosing cheaper batteries would make particular sense for an application targeting more budget-conscious buyers.

Mercedes already demonstrates how this can work within one lineup. The electric CLA—likely a direct rival to BMW’s upcoming cheaper Neue Klasse EV—has a larger 85-kWh battery option with NMC chemistry, plus an entry-level variant that gets a 58-kWh LFP pack. Buyers can choose between a lower entry price and the extra range offered by the bigger battery, without switching to an entirely different car.

Meanwhile, BMW is expanding where its battery cells come from. It announced a deal with Samsung SDI to supply Gen6 cells from Europe and LG Energy Solution from the U.S., starting toward the end of the decade. Samsung joins CATL and EVE Energy in BMW’s European cell supply network, although none of these agreements identify the cells they will supply as LFP.

BMW’s cheaper chemistry could help contain costs, but the badge will still fetch a premium, so it will likely still be more expensive than similar offerings from mainstream brands.

#4436. Gift Guide: Best Tech and Gadgets for Gearheads and Car Lovers

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Keep up with the latest automotive and garage tech with our picks for the best gadgets and tech on the market today.

This article was updated in November 2026.

Automotive enthusiasm has always gone hand in hand with a fascination for technology. At Road & Track, we’re always interested in the technology that makes the automotive experience better.

Some are practical necessities, others are just plain cool, but each has something to offer a car enthusiast. Think diagnostic scanners, GPS navigation systems, performance monitors, wireless phone accessories, and clever tools that help tackle jobs around the garage.

We’ve included options at various price points and for different kinds of enthusiasts, so you can find something useful, interesting, and worth keeping in the toolbox.

The Mission 1 Pro is built for capturing the kind of driving footage that makes you want to take the long way home. I recently used one myself on a drive up the Pacific Coast Highway, where its compact size made it easy to bring along and its high-resolution video captured everything from sweeping coastal views to the little details along the road. It’s a versatile action camera for car enthusiasts who want more than a few phone clips from their next road trip, with the rugged, portable design GoPro has built its reputation on.

The Cobra RAD 700i is less a radar detector and more a digital co-pilot for the fast lane. With long-range detection, GPS-powered AutoLearn filtering, and Bluetooth connectivity to Cobra’s Drive Smarter network, it helps cut through false alerts while keeping you tuned into live speed traps, cameras, and roadside hazards. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility sweeten the deal, turning your windshield into mission control for highway miles and heavy right feet.

A navigation app is only as useful as the cellular connection behind it, and that can become a problem once you get far enough outside town. The weBoost Drive X is a multi-user cellular signal booster that uses an external magnetic-mount antenna to capture available signals, then amplifies them for devices inside the cabin. Its amplifier delivers up to 50 dB of gain and supports several major U.S. cellular frequency bands. The kit includes both exterior and interior antennas, a power supply, and the amplifier itself, making it a worthwhile consideration for road trippers, overlanders, and anyone who regularly ventures beyond reliable cell coverage.

Running navigation, streaming music, and charging wirelessly can turn a smartphone into a little pocket-size space heater, especially on a summer road trip. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 combines a magnetic Qi2 charging mount with an integrated cooling fan designed to help manage device temperatures during longer drives. It supports wireless charging at up to 15 watts, includes an adjustable air-vent mount, and uses a multicolor LED indicator to show charging status.

A phone running Google Maps isn’t going to cut it when the pavement ends and the trail network gets complicated. The Garmin Tread 2 Overland Edition is an eight-inch, glove-friendly GPS navigator built specifically for off-road travel, with preloaded topographic maps of North and South America, public-land information, and U.S. Forest Service Motor Vehicle Use Maps. Its IP67-rated enclosure is designed to withstand dust, water exposure, and rough conditions, while the included magnetic-assisted locking mount secures the unit to the dashboard. It also supports downloadable satellite imagery and route planning through Garmin’s Tread app, giving overlanders a much more capable navigation setup than a smartphone alone.

The BlueDriver Bluetooth Pro OBD2 Scanner is a compact diagnostic tool that plugs into a vehicle’s OBD-II port and sends information wirelessly to an iOS or Android device. Beyond reading and clearing standard check-engine codes, it offers enhanced diagnostics for systems such as ABS, airbags, transmission, and TPMS on supported vehicles. The companion app also provides live sensor data, Mode 6 test results, and repair reports with possible causes and reported fixes. With compatibility covering most 1996-and-newer North American vehicles and no subscription fees, it’s a useful step up from a basic code reader for anyone who likes doing their own troubleshooting.

A stopwatch can tell you whether your last lap was faster, but it won’t explain why. The Garmin Catalyst is a dedicated track-driving analysis system that combines a 10Hz multi-GNSS receiver, onboard accelerometers and gyroscopes, and an HD remote camera to record and evaluate a driver’s performance. Garmin’s True Track Positioning technology analyzes racing lines, braking points, apexes, and track-out positions, while its True Optimal Lap feature combines the best sections of recorded laps to show how much time is potentially left on the table. It can also deliver real-time audio coaching, making it a particularly interesting tool for track-day drivers who want to improve without investing in a complicated professional data-logging setup.

DJI’s Mini 4 Pro is packed full of impressive imaging capabilities and innovative navigation features. The 249-gram weight of the unit means the device is just under the Federal Aviation Administration’s 250-gram limit for registering your drone in the United States, significantly reducing the barriers to entry other drones require. The Mini 4 Pro captures 4K video at up to 100 frames per second (fps) or 4K at 60 fps with HDR video. The unit is rated for roughly 12 miles of transmission between the drone and the included remote, ensuring even congested areas or valleys/hills won’t impact your ability to record video or snap photos. Other features include 360-degree obstacle-avoidance sensors, a plethora of automated capture modes capable of locking in on and tracking subjects, and a 34-minute flight time with the included batteries.

Stop stuffing your pockets with multiple flashlights when you really just need this one. Holding the ArkPro Ultra feels immediately different than a standard flashlight; the flat, slim profile disappears in your pocket or EDC bag unlike bulky round tubes, yet the unibody aluminum feels incredibly dense and premium in the hand. It solves the biggest headache of carrying high-tech gear: charging anxiety. Because it finally supports both magnetic snap-charging and standard USB-C, you can top it off on your nightstand or with a laptop cable without hunting for a proprietary cord. Whether you are running a presentation or checking for leaks under a car, it feels like the Swiss Army knife of light that actually performs as well as the dedicated tools it replaces.

The IntelliDash Pro X10 is a modern shortcut for aging dashboards—a slim 10-inch touchscreen that brings wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto to just about any car without surgery, swearing, or a weekend in the garage. Setup is gloriously plug-and-play, with Bluetooth, FM, AUX, and voice-assistant support baked in. Big maps, brighter road trips, cleaner cable chaos. It’s the kind of upgrade that makes a 2009 commuter vehicle feel a little more spaceship.

A shiny new paint job can hide a lot of history, particularly on an older car that’s been through a few owners and at least one body shop. The Rdinscos Car Coating Thickness Meter is designed to measure the thickness of paint and other coatings on metal panels, giving buyers a way to compare readings across a vehicle’s bodywork. Uneven measurements can point toward previous refinishing, additional layers of paint, or body filler, making the tool particularly useful when inspecting a potential project or evaluating a used-car purchase. It’s not a replacement for a trained eye or a proper pre-purchase inspection, but it can help uncover evidence of repairs that a quick walkaround might miss.

The Hoto Tools Precision Screwdriver Kit Pro is a wonderful gift for any DIY aficionado or professional. The screwdriver uses a two-gear design to provide more than enough torque for delicate builds or repairs. It also features built-in LED lights and an innovative contact charging case that stores the drill and its accessories, ensuring power is always topped off when needed.

This kit isn’t just about looks—it’s about substance, with 48 bits forged from S2 steel, complemented by a suite of practical tools like spudgers, tweezers, and a suction cup for those tricky parts. The electric screwdriver’s adjustable torque and handy magnetizer/demagnetizer tool help to ensure no small bits and pieces go missing. Whether you’re a tech enthusiast or a creative tinkerer, the Hoto Tools kit provides practicality and precision in a compact, stylish package.

Built for gloveboxes, road trips, and “oh no” moments, the Vantrue JS3 is a compact four-in-one roadside powerhouse: jump starter, air compressor, fast-charging power bank, and emergency light, in one rugged shell. With a 3250-amp peak current, 160-psi inflator, and USB-C PD 65-watt charging, it’s designed to revive dead batteries, refill tires fast, and keep devices alive when the highway gets unpredictable. Think of it as roadside insurance with a lithium heartbeat.

Shopping for someone who already has every gadget is tough, but the Insta360 X6 is a guaranteed win. Because it shoots in every direction at once, you don’t even have to worry about framing—just hit record and pick the best angles later on your phone. The software automatically edits out the selfie stick, making it look like a low-flying drone is following you, whether you’re carving up back roads, hitting the mountain bike trails, or just messing around in the backyard. It’s incredibly easy to use and makes literally any activity look epic.

Reverse-engineering a custom intake manifold or replicating a classic car’s unobtainium trim pieces usually means dragging a fragile laptop into the grime of the garage. The Creality Sermoon P1 standalone 3-D scanner finally severs that tether. This isn’t some plastic hobbyist toy; it’s a high-octane engineering workstation crammed into a handheld chassis. Packing a Qualcomm 8-core processor and a massive 24GB of RAM, the P1 processes dense 3-D meshes directly on its crisp six-inch touchscreen. It boasts enough onboard horsepower to digitize a complete engine block without breaking a single drop of digital sweat. For the uncompromising gearhead looking to turn physical metal into flawless digital data, the Sermoon P1 is the ultimate garage weapon.

This cordless four-in-one Slim V8 Apex mini vacuum packs 19,000Pa suction into a glovebox-friendly frame, with attachments for crumbs, cupholders, keyboards, pet hair, and other chaos agents. It also blows, inflates, and pumps, making it equal parts detail tool and travel sidekick. Lightweight, USB-C rechargeable, and surprisingly mighty, it’s built for people who treat messes like pit stops—not permanent conditions.

The Nextmug Go is the kind of gadget that quietly upgrades your entire morning ritual. This sleek, self-heating travel mug keeps coffee or tea at your preferred temperature — Warm, Hot, or Piping — for hours, so every sip tastes freshly poured. Its spill-resistant lid, long-lasting battery, and app-free controls make it refreshingly simple to use on commutes, road trips, or marathon workdays. Think of it as a thermos with a master’s degree in modern convenience.

HoverAir’s X1 ProMax is the ultimate drone for people who don’t know anything about drones. This self-flying, fully enclosed camera launches from your hand and uses 10+ AI-powered shooting and follow modes to capture photographs and up to 8K/30 (or 4K/120) video, stabilized by SmoothCapture 2.0—a two-axis gimbal with electronic image stabilization (EIS) and horizon leveling. It’ll track confidently with a rated 42 km/h (26 mph) follow speed, and its OmniTerrain feature is designed for flying near water, snow, and other tricky surfaces. I’ve shot various drones over the years, and while others might be more technically capable, none are as simple to use as the ProMax. The best part is, it’ll fit nearly anywhere. It’s a no-brainer for anyone who wants to capture drone footage quickly in a device that folds up smaller than most books.

Ride1Up’s Revv 1 DRT is a moped-style e-bike that trades Lycra vibes for dirt-track energy. A 52-volt system feeds a 1000-watt Bafang rear hub and a 35-amp controller with a “boost” party trick, while a 52-vole/20-Ah UL-certified pack (about 1040 watt-hours) keeps the lights on. Off-road mode unlocks 28-plus mph for private property, and the chassis gets real hardware: a 150-mm dual-crown fork, 76 mm of rear travel, and flur-piston hydraulic stoppers. Range is quoted at 30–60 miles, and the whole package carries UL 2849/2271 safety certifications—welcome peace of mind on a 30-mph pseudo-moto.

On trail or torn-up alleys, the DRT feels like a small, electric pit bike: confident, quick to squirt, and more fun than it has any right to be. The flip side is familiar: short cranks and moped geometry make real pedaling an afterthought, knobby 20-by-fours hum and nibble at range, and you’ll want to mind local laws before touching that off-road setting. At $2395, it undercuts many fashion-forward rivals while delivering genuine off-road chops and useful kit (headlight fairing, molle mounting, twist throttle). If your commute occasionally turns to dirt, this is the hooligan commuter to beat.

Wolfbox’s G840S is the kind of upgrade that makes an older car feel quietly futuristic. This 12-inch smart-mirror dash cam layers 4K front recording, a rear backup camera, GPS tracking, parking assistance, and touchscreen controls into a sleek rearview mirror replacement. The wide-angle rear feed also helps tame blind spots—especially handy in crowded garages and tight parking decks. #4435. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#4433. Land Rover Is Going After BYD Over This Alleged Defender Lookalike: Report

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Court-appointed bailiffs reportedly raided two BYD offices on behalf of Jaguar Land Rover. The issue? JLR reportedly has a problem with the Chinese automaker's Ti7, alleging that it infringes on the UK-based firm's intellectual property.

The Times reports that two BYD offices in the Netherlands were raided back in August over the alleged copycat model. During the raid, bailiffs seized digital records related to the development of the Ti7. According to the report, a Dutch court will decide later this week whether JLR's claims against BYD can proceed. The Ti7 should reach European customers soon.

Both BYD and JLR declined to comment when reached by InsideEVs sister site Motor1.

Visually, the similarities between the the BYD Ti7 and Land Rover Defender aren't hard to understand. But there might be more to it than just BYD having a similar boxy styling. According to The Times, JLR suspects that engineers at BYD may have dismantled and reverse engineered a Defender as part of the R&D process.

That alone isn't really an uncommon practice. Heck, any automaker worth its salt benchmarks models from competitors. But if BYD used any of that proprietary and protected tech in the production version of the Ti7, it could be a bigger problem.

BYD originally launched the Ti7 in China in September 2025 starting at under $27,000. It released a battery-electric back in April for $29,900 and plans to begin delivering the Ti7 in Europe as early as January.

European versions of the Ti7 start at around $64,500 versus the comparable 7-seater version of the Land Rover Defender 110 running nearly $92,000. Naturally, you can see why JRL might be a bit miffed about BYD coming to market in Europe with the Ti7.

This also isn't unexplored territory for JLR. It's been down the litigious path before to defend its IP against other automakers—namely British automaker Ineos and Chinese brand Jiangling. While it lost the case against Ineos, it did win the 2019 legal battle against Jiangling, finding that its Landwind X7 was too similar to the Range Rover Evoque.

#4432. Honda Investing $3 Billion to Build New Ohio Factory, Increase Hybrid Production in U.S.

The new plant will be capable of producing 240,000 vehicles a year, and multiple new models are currently under development.

Audi may have recently announced its first-ever U.S. production facility, but at least one Japanese automaker with a head start in that race doesn’t seem keen on giving up any places. On Monday, Honda announced it is investing $3 billion in a new central Ohio factory; the plant, which will produce up to 240,000 vehicles annually, is expected to be online by 2029.

Now, with nine production facilities across the U.S., Honda is no stranger to domestic production, but the new factory plan goes beyond merely adding production capacity. Instead, the company is targeting increased production of hybrid-electric vehicles and their accompanying drivetrain parts. The new plant will sit between Honda’s current East Liberty and Marysville Auto Plants, the carmaker said, and will focus on multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid and battery-electric vehicles. Honda said the plant will be one of the most advanced factories in the world, leveraging leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

"As Honda approaches 50 years of building products close to our customers in America, we are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years,” said Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “These investments strengthen America’s role as a cornerstone of Honda’s global future and reflect our confidence in our more than 30,000 Honda associates and the strength of American manufacturing. By expanding our comprehensive R&D and manufacturing capabilities, we will be better positioned to serve our customers and contribute to the economic vitality of the communities where we operate.”

Building another plant in Ohio was an easy choice for Honda. Honda’s U.S. supply base is nearby, and the automaker has a strong reputation among the region’s skilled workforce. The Japanese automaker has previously committed to launching 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030; North America is the target for many of these models, which are currently in development at R&D facilities in California and Ohio. All told, Honda said the new plant will increase its annual U.S. production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles a year.

The company’s Alabama Auto Plant will also receive new investment to expand engine production for a new V-6 hybrid engine; Honda will retool the engine production facility and one of the production lines to accommodate Passport SUV production. The Anna Engine Plant in Ohio will also be retooled, to produce a next-generation 4-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine for future compact and midsize vehicles built in North America. Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio will be retooled for two next-generation Honda Hybrid systems in compact vehicles, while Honda Transmission Plant-Georgia will be retooled for next-generation hybrid systems in larger vehicles. All this retooling will account for a 250-percent increase in hybrid powertrain system capacity in Ohio.

“Honda's leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” said Ohio governor Mike DeWine. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda's manufacturing lines. Today's announcement isn't just an investment in a new facility—it's an investment in Ohio's people and Ohio's future.”

#4431. The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.
