#4405. Rewarding for the Right Owner: 1979 Lancia Zagato Tested

The car for those who view eccentricity as a virtue and fun as a necessity.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

“ZAG-uh-toe .... What is that, one of them new little Plymouths?”

He’d been studying the little Lancia through the window as we rummaged through his parts store in search of a you-wire-it cigarette lighter we could graft into the car’s electrical system. The on-board lighter socket had proved incompatible with our Escort’s plug.

“Za-GAH-toe,” we corrected. “It's made in Italy.”

He considered that piece of informa­tion as we paid for the lighter, then tried to sell us a can of engine additive as we made for the door. The dogeared display for the pour-in miracle claimed it would do everything short of putting you in the winner’s circle at Daytona. In the old days, in different packaging, it probably sold as a cure for rheumatism, lice, warts, heaves, halitosis, and hard hearing. He patted the uppermost can and his voice trailed us into the drizzly afternoon, hinting of impending doom.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07011

He had a point there, but we forsook the additive and let the door close be­hind us. We hooked up the Escort and set out into the growing evening rain­storm in search of a major mechanical or electrical failure to get pissed off about. The further we got from Dayto­na, spearing out into the chilly, desert­ed, water-swept two-lanes of central Florida, howling into the gloom at a steady 80, the clearer our second thoughts became. What if Lancia’s self­-incriminating talk of a “new high-quali­ty modular electrical system through­out” was just a hoax? We didn’t even have an umbrella. Would the modular electrics leave us sinking in the middle of some non-modular backwater swamp? Would the shift linkage come adrift? Would the carburetion cease to carburet, or the ignition cease to ignite? These were fits of pique visited upon us by Lancias before. But the Zagato did none of the above. Oh, the letdown, not to be able to tell you we had to hitch­hike out of the Glades in the back of a sagging half-ton Ford pickup.

Times have apparently changed at Lancia. While we can’t say the thrashing we dealt our Zagato was the equivalent of 50,000 miles’ worth of normal driv­ing, the car suffered us, if not gladly, at least with no crippling catastrophes. Its shortcomings fell more in the area of nuisance value, an area offset by the fun of driving the car under the right cir­cumstances. As often happens with cars of strong character, the Zagato’s car-to-­owner-to-car relationship becomes a high-spirited adversary relationship, an exchange of sometimes conflicting, sometime parallel philosophies. This re­lationship can make a Lancia Zagato a rewarding car for the right owner. All that remains is to determine whether ownership then qualifies him as a 24-ka­rat eccentric in good standing, or simply a lover of good fun.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07011

Fun is what Lancia had in mind when it contracted Carrozzeria Zagato to cre­ate and build a coachbuilt steel targa body for the existing Beta Coupe. The unit-bodied result is an interesting com­bination of a normal lift-off fiberglass targa roof panel and an everyday roadster’s fold-down vinyl rear roof and plastic window. The targa bar that re­mains after everything else is lifted off or folded down provides sturdy rollover protection, enhanced by horizontal out­er roofline struts that connect the bar with the windshield pillars. Four configurations are possible by adding or re­moving the roof components and roll­ing windows up or down.

The resulting greenhouse possesses all the elegance of a railroad shanty and thwarts the clean, simple lines of the lower body. From certain angles, the Zagato looks like a stubby El Camino pickup with an enclosed bed, but unlike an El Camino, it has another pair of seats behind the driver and the number­-one passenger. However, candidates for travel in back may want to suggest a democratic drawing of straws, fearing their upper and lower extremities will be forever molded into unnatural shapes. Lowering the back window pro­vides a modern version of the rumble seat and a bit more headroom, but no extra sympathy for the legs. The Zagato is not by any means or intent an appro­priate way to transport half your neigh­borhood to a formal dinner party. Con­sider it a sports car that happens to ben­efit from a slight extra people-carrying capacity suited to quick runs down to the beach, the movies, or the local wa­tering hole.

As always, Lancia has provided a nice setting for front-seat travelers, creating a modern environment that welcomes you with comfort—though the passen­ger is probably more comfortable than the driver. The seats are good, but the driver is squeezed into the classic Amer­ican-knees-in-the-American-armpits Italian driving position, arms stretching for a steering wheel that lies out near the horizon.

But inside the car, you tend to forget about the varied points of styling and sometimes even about the peculiar driv­ing position. Sometimes the Zagato is so much fun you can’t help yourself. Other people watch you rip past, and you know they’re thinking, “What would I do if I had that? What does it feel like without a roof or a back win­dow?” They figure anything with these looks must be kinda fast, and they won­der how many friends you can squeeze into the thing before the cops stop you. The Zagato is meant for the unpredict­able kind of fun you can have only if you’re unpredictable enough to have a car like this. If that’s eccentric, so be it.

The Zagato’s chassis configuration has become so commonplace as to have lost all appeal for eccentrics. Contained within the 92.5-inch wheelbase and 164.6-inch overall length are the trans­verse engine and front-wheel drive shared with Lancia’s other models, and echoed by a dozen other manufacturers. A five-speed manual or a new three-­speed automatic transmission provides the gearing, and the engine, provided by parent company Fiat, has been en­larged for all Lancia’s models this year, jumping from 1756 cc to 1995 cc. The 84.0 mm bore remains the same, but the stroke has been increased from 79.2 to 90.0 mm. The two-liter whips out 87 horsepower at an enthusiastic 5400 rpm and boasts a torque increase of almost 17 percent, up to 105 pound-feet at 2900 rpm. The double-overhead-cam four leans over twenty degrees, and its electronic ignition, Weber two-barrel carburetor, and aluminum hemi-heads provide both exotic specifications and good midrange performance. The en­gine runs on unleaded gas, purifies its wastes with a catalytic converter, and, when hitched to the five-speed over­drive, propels the Zagato an average of 19 miles per gallon.

At 2730 pounds, the Zagato is heavy for a car its size. Its standard high nu­merical gearing is necessary for lively around-town and back-road perform­ance, but it produces much noisy com­plaint from the engine in the lower gears. Fourth gear above 60 is hopelessly noisy even though it has another 27 mph worth of revs left. Fifth ceases the caterwauling up to about 70 mph, when droning sets in and wind noise around the roof panel and rear window increas­es to what seem supersonic levels. Noisy and tightly wound though it might be, the wailing little engine produces only mid-pack performance—0 to 60 mph in 11.9 seconds, the quarter-mile in 18.7 seconds at 73 mph. By standing on the gas long enough, you can wring a 103-mph top speed out of the Zagato. Its passing performance is quite reassuring when you’ve picked the right gear. On occasion, getting the right gear can be much more a bother than picking it, but the transaxle’s linkage isn’t entirely bad, and the fat shift knob and easy heel­-and-toe movement are fine. The five­-speed pattern is a proper H, with fifth up and away, opposite reverse.

The brakes Lancia has hung under the coachwork are more than just reas­suring. With a big disc at every hand­some alloy wheel, and aggressive, low­-profile Pirelli P6s, the Zagato likes nothing better than knocking off speed with breathtaking quickness and control. The speedometer needle struggles to keep up in getting down. Pedal effort is light, and the rousing 186-foot mea­surement for 70-to-0-mph stops runs neck-and-neck with or even betters some of the world’s highest-performance automobiles.

The 185/65R-14 P6 Pirellis are tre­mendous. Not only do they ride smoothly and quietly, even at the high pressures we use for hard running, they’re beyond reproach in their per­formance characteristics. They are pre­dictable, precise, and monumental in their ability to inspire confidence. They seem to have no sudden tuck-under, and finding their limit seems almost as much a mental exercise as a physical one. While the Pirellis are good, the Za­gato certainly adds its own zesty spice to the handling brew. The spring and shock rates provide a firm smoothness of control. The car’s aloof road man­ners do not disappear into the lower re­cesses of every chuckhole or flutter over every sudden rise. The suspension is all-independent, MacPherson struts all around. Each aspect of wheel control is dovetailed neatly with the others, from the point where the P6s manhandle the pavement right up to the precise, re­fined new rack-and-pinion power steer­ing, which allows only slight tugs on the wheel in the lower gears. If it were not for the power assist, the awkwardly positioned steering wheel would be a real obstacle, more opponent than ac­complice in the battle of leverage. Its rake adjustment allows none of the fore­-and-aft movement so badly needed for correct reach to the wheel.

Directional stability is outstanding, the Zagato arrowing its way over and through every snide parlor trick our grousing malcontent of a highway system can throw at it. The inherent understeer is moderate, and its symptoms are fur­ther reduced by the quick steering and the response of the Pirellis. Body roll and brake dive are under tight rein. The car works not as a scurvy rat's nest of separate parts, but as one very snug unit.

Lancia hasn’t been exactly famous for well-conceived interiors, but the Zagato benefits from a general redesign for 1979. Our white test car, trimmed in black and sporting the new bumpers and restyled grille and hood introduced this year on the older Beta Coupe, was cloaked inside with gray cut-pile carpet and black leather. The dash, also black, contains a new, six-gauge instrument panel. A 120-mph speedometer and a 7000-rpm tachometer, redlined at 6500, dominate the scene, even though they’re partly hidden behind the over­styled wheel, which has miserably placed spokes. Smaller gauges keep tabs on amps, fuel, and water temp, the oth­er three being allotted to the oil pres­sure, temperature, and level. Our water­-temp gauge wasn’t registering, so that must have meant we didn't have any . . . what, water or temp? The layout is clut­tered around the nacelle for the radio (which is very good and has a power an­tenna), but the general ergonomics and labeling of controls are excellent. The ventilation, heater, and air conditioning worked very well, handling unexpected Florida extremes in a manner obtrusive only because such adroitness was a sur­prise in a newly introduced limited-pro­duction car.

Several irritating bugaboos crop up here and there around the Zagato to take the edge off the nicer sides of its personality. A horrid “modesty panel” (the biz name for the under-dash trim panel that hides a car’s plumbing and wiring woes from critical eyes) snaps at your toes every time you press the clutch pedal, solidly and dangerously snagging your shoe as you let the pedal back out. The sun visors cannot be fold­ed to the sides. The shoulder harness has a tendency to tangle. The plastic rear window is clouded with a chemical haze. The rear-view mirror vibrates. The glove-box door fits poorly and is blemished with a bright blue “Unleaded Fuel Only” badge. And the hardware and trim don’t equal the excellent over­all paint and finish.

The Zagato, at a base price of $10,811, is about 1300 clams up on the Beta Coupe from which it springs. If its price isn’t enough to guarantee exclu­sivity to the eccentrics in its future, its availability will be: fewer than 1500 Za­gatos will be sold here. For those who can’t bear the thought of showing up at the same party with identical designer originals, a Special Edition Zagato, gild­ed in black paint, gold striping, unique emblems, and black interior, will be marketed at $11,800. Only 250 of these will find their way in.

Now all the U.S. Lancia dealers have to do is find a crowd of young, wind-in-­the-hair eccentrics who like to have fun driving fast with a carload of outdoorsy blondes over perfectly awful roads that don’t demand a lot of horsepower. Piece of cake. But they should beware of a potential buyer who sidles up looking for one of them new little Plymouths. He really just wants to unload some en­gine additive that, in a pinch, can cure hard hearing, halitosis, heaves, warts, lice, and rheumatism.

#4404. Tesla Cybertruck had its best month in over a year. It’s still going away

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

#4403. The AI Boom Is Creating A New Supply Chain Headache For Automakers

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The auto industry may be headed for another chip crunch. Last time, it was the pandemic that snarled supply chains and threw the chip market out of whack. This time, the AI boom is squeezing the supply of the basic semiconductors that modern cars rely on.

The CEO of Dutch semiconductor manufacturer Nexperia, Stefan Tilger, told Reuters that competitors had shifted supply for commodity semiconductors toward chips used in AI data center. And since a great deal of that production was once dedicated to mature chips (like those used in cars and other industrial equipment), a bottleneck is quickly brewing in the automotive supply chain. The auto industry is "suffering quite heavily," he said.

STMicroelectronics, a Swiss semiconductor manufacturer, is seeing the same problem, according to comments reported by the outlet. CEO Jean-Marc Chery warns that chip foundries and assembly plants are increasingly "disengaging" from traditional mainstream automotive and industrial applications. Tilger says that another emerging area eating into the supply chain is the new breed of robotics beginning to hit the market.

Both company leaders are stressing that the upcoming shortage isn't because big GPU companies like Nvidia are eating up every last chip known to man. The squeeze is happening even further upstream in the supply chain.

And the auto industry is already feeling the impact. German automotive supplier Aumovio, which makes sensors, cameras, and other in-vehicle electronics for customers like BYD, BMW, and Ford, warned on a recent earnings call that its chip costs are rising and will "explode" next year.

"What is the reason for that situation? The reason are the data centers for mainly artificial intelligence," said interim finance head Claus Bauer. "We can tell you that there's no price sensitivity whatsoever in that area. All of our suppliers in that regard could sell twice their capacity to this very lucrative, non-price-sensitive area."

Automakers are no strangers to semiconductor shortages. During the pandemic, chip shortages forced car companies to idle production lines and even ship cars without certain computer-reliant features, like automatic start/stop. It's not clear yet that things will get as bad as last time. But if they do, the AI-driven race to make everything smarter could lead to less-smart cars, if only temporarily.

#4400. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”

He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

#4399. This New Electric Paver Can Lay Down 1,200 Tonnes Of Asphalt A Day

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The construction world is getting quieter by the day, thanks to the gradual electrification of big rigs traditionally powered by diesel engines. After trucks, diggers, and cranes, asphalt pavers are now going electric.

Switzerland’s Ammann, which is known for its asphalt and concrete plant equipment, has transformed one of its mainstream diesel asphalt pavers to run on electric power. Thanks to a Volvo Penta powertrain, the eABG 4820 is now one of the largest electric pavers on the market, capable of laying up to 500 tonnes per hour and a maximum output of 1,200 tonnes per day with a charging stop.

Without intermediate charging, the machine can put down between 350 and 450 tonnes of asphalt.

Before getting into the details, the biggest advantage of an electric paver over a diesel rig is the significantly lower noise output. A 99-kilowatt electric motor is powered by a massive 270–kilowatt-hour battery pack arranged in three separate units. Volvo Penta supplies the batteries, motors, power electronics, and control technology, while Ammann used its expertise in hydraulic-powered machinery to put it all together.

“It comes down to energy management and architecture,” said Philipp Bramer, head of the e-paver development team at Ammann. “The electric driveline doesn’t just power the machine. It communicates seamlessly with the hydraulics. Simultaneously, the intelligent control system makes sure that the system supplies exactly the right amount of energy to the machine.”

The nickel-cobalt-aluminum oxide (NCA) traction batteries can be charged from a CCS2 connector at up to 150 kW in roughly one and a half hours, while AC charging at up to 22 kW can replenish the battery in 12 hours. Amman says that the battery provides enough juice for an entire work shift, but that an external power supply is responsible for its proprietary ABG e+ screed heat system.

The electric paver can handle widths of up to 21.3 feet (6.5 meters), making it a good choice for most paving scenarios, especially in emission- and noise-sensitive job sites. We’ve all seen and heard a diesel asphalt paver in operation—I vividly remember when the street I grew up on got its first layer of asphalt decades ago, and while I was fascinated by all the machinery, I still remember that the site was extremely loud.

This, coupled with the fact that an electric paver emits up to 70% less carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, should make diesel construction equipment a thing of the past—at least in crowded, already polluted urban areas.

What’s more, because an electric powertrain has significantly fewer moving parts compared to a diesel lump, a lot of maintenance tasks simply disappear, along with their associated costs. At the same time, though, construction companies need to install charging equipment at their depots and find ways of topping up their rigs on the jobsite.

#4398. Kia launches two new PV5 electric van variants in the UK

Kia opened orders for two new PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

Kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia said, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also launched the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The new variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

It’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

#4397. 8 Best Weapons in COD Modern Warfare 4 Multiplayer

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

It's that time of the year again when an annual Call of Duty launch has taken over everyone’s schedule, or at least alongside a renowned Zelda game at the moment. And for someone like me who’s dabbled in and out of modern releases from both Infinity Ward and Treyarch, the former has genuinely done a marvelous job with COD: Modern Warfare 4, making it one of the best releases in the franchise yet.

And despite my competitive nature subsiding since then, the COD Multiplayer gremlin teenager part of me never died, and so I’ve stuck around with MW4’s multiplayer. I load into a lobby feeling confident, then either get absolutely flattened or dominate with my team—no in-between.

This is DualShockers' review of COD: Modern Warfare 4, covering all the ins and outs of the campaign, multiplayer, and the new DMZ Extraction Mode.

The weapons matter equally with your game sense and skill here, since some feel amazing the second you pick them while others just don’t suit a certain playstyle. I’ve burned a few hours (and a lot of attachments) figuring out which is which, and I’d rather save you the trouble.

So I implore you to stick around today because whether you’re grinding for camos or just want to stop getting melted in Hardpoint, here are the best weapons to use in Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer.

Note: This list is being drafted as of Season 1’s patch notes in MW4.

I’m kicking us off with a gun that’s had a divided reception lately from both other players and a couple of my closest friends who play with me.

The Nyx is a flanker’s SMG since it’s quick enough to catch people off guard when you come in from the side or behind. But I’d be lying if I didn’t mention how it can feel like a pea-shooter compared to the other SMGs that outclass it.

Its performance has improved following the Season 1 balancing changes, which increased its second medium-damage profile from 15 to 16 and its minimum damage from 13 to 14.

I mean, that (sort of) makes it more forgiving outside its ideal close-range engagements, but yeah, it's still worth including as an alternative for someone who wants something different in MW4’s multiplayer, especially if they’re a run-and-gun player, since this SMG works wonders in that regard. It's also a fun close-range SMG to use in Hardcore game modes, where other guns can one-shot you easily.

Grinding enough in the early levels to unlock the Axion was worth it, because this AR deserves more recognition here as an ol’ reliable gun, especially after its recent improvements, where you can’t go wrong picking it for a loadout. Its Season 1 improvements have increased its medium damage range by 11% and muzzle velocity by 13%.

So this ends up making it much more dependable when challenging enemy players across longer sightlines or off-angles, which matters especially on larger multiplayer maps. If you’re on controller, try to dial the recoil down with the attachments; otherwise, get more range and ADS speed/stability on this bad boy, and it will hit like a truck in the right hands, trust me.

And speaking of hitting like a truck, if you want an AR that quite literally embodies that term, then look no further than the Kastov 762. Its biggest advantage is its damage output, especially when holding longer sightlines or on players in close-to-medium range. It's another weapon with a mixed fanbase, but if you don’t mind the slower fire rate, add it to one of your loadout arsenals immediately.

Also, the latest S1 balancing update matters: the weapon received a 4% increase to its medium damage, a 5% improvement to its medium damage range, and additional head, neck, and upper-torso damage multipliers. Also, if you’re one of the majority who finds this weapon hard to control, you can try the FSS Fireline Grip as an alternative underbarrel attachment.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer has arrived, and it features skill-based matchmaking, with no Open Matchmaking playlist options in sight.

As someone who absolutely adored his Pulse Rifles from Destiny, or even the BR55 from Halo 2, the Hyeon Burst in MW4 immediately became one of my favorite weapons to use, even if it's a bit of an annoyance against some of the faster TTK weapons.

It also ends up rewarding those players who can maintain their accuracy rather than simply holding down the trigger and hoping for the best. In the S1 patch notes, the Hyeon Hyperburst Apex attachment took a sizeable nerf, losing 23% of its maximum damage and 20% of its minimum damage. But you do get compensated since the regular Hyeon also received a small medium-damage buff.

I already know every weapon pick you off in Hardcore, but Hyeon Burst is so fun on its own here, with the 3-burst fire letting you pick off multiple targets from a safe distance. Keep in mind that while the Hyperburst attachment increases fire rate by 23%, it also adds a fair bit of horizontal kick, so if that’s a deal-breaker, take it off and use something else that won’t make it hard to use.

One of the earliest SMGs you can unlock is the ISO Nightshade. If the VEL 46 is for the aggressive players, the Nightshade is for everyone else. It kills nearly as fast up close, but it’s much easier to control, so you stay accurate when fights get messy while rushing.

And much like the rest of the aforementioned weapons on this list, it has also benefited from the latest weapon balancing changes, receiving an 11% increase to its maximum damage range alongside a 9% increase to its minimum damage, which is genuinely a welcome improvement for a weapon that I think previously relied heavily on making you get close to opponents.

With the Nightshade, you can use it at medium range and make it a hybrid run-and-gun playstyle with fast ADS and minimal sway. I also recommend mastering a hip-fire style with it since Modern Warfare 4’s hip-fire integration is actually very forgiving, at least in my experience. But hey, if that’s not your forte, totally fine; I’d just stick with making this an agile weapon for yourself.

I love using my MP7s across various shooting games whenever given the chance, so imagine my love at first sight when I picked up the Vel 46 and ran wild with it on the Transit 213 Map. Mixed opinions on the map aside, the VEL 46 is one of the best aggressive guns to grace MW4's multiplayer meta.

Its excellent close-range performance makes it extremely effective for rushing objectives or catching enemy players off-guard when they least expect it. And obviously, I don’t have to explain that its main drawback is its limited range, so don't even try to use it in lanes or main angles.

Interestingly, the Season 1 patch slightly reduced its maximum and intermediate damage ranges but increased its minimum damage from 13 to 14, so the bottom line is that it barely changed, and you can still use it as a meta option or even just a fun run-and-gun weapon.

The VEL 46 Snap Apex attachment is a must, and you should try to go all out on faster ADS and movement speed. One last pro tip: use the Ninja perk on this, or any other SMG build, so you can flank without making noise from your footsteps.

Introduced with Season 1, the Cronen Osprey is arguably one of the most exciting recent additions to the weapon roster, and it deserves serious consideration if you’re not already trying it out in your loadouts. That’s because it has an exceptionally fast fire rate and accuracy that makes it feel almost like a laser.

The Osprey is built around speed, so it fires very quickly, which makes it deadly when it connects and awkward when it doesn’t, because the recoil climbs and drifts sideways if you hold the trigger on the controller.

The trick is to fire in controlled bursts and add attachments that steady it without slowing your aim, since fast handling is a big part of why it’s worth using. The recoil is otherwise very manageable on keyboard, so I’d advise sticking with anything that gives you faster ADS or a wider damage-output range.

Finally, we come to one of the most popular weapons in Modern Warfare 4: the M4. It’s a weapon that you just can’t go wrong choosing, especially if you’re just jumping into the game’s multiplayer scene. I mean, that’s probably why I keep seeing other players bring it up in community discussions: it is fast, reliable, and easy to get comfortable with.

And the cherry on top is how the Season 1 update has made it even more appealing, increasing its maximum damage range by 8% and its headshot multiplier by 4%. But we’re not done here: by equipping the Apex attachment, you can practically transform the M4 into an SMG variant that's extremely viable at close range or for running and gunning, without feeling like a middle-ground weapon.

Keep in mind that this removes the option to change some other attachments, so if you feel like the Apex hinders the weapon’s viability for you, stick to the normal variant and make it feel as snazzy as possible without recoil or slow handling.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

#4395. Future Cars Worth Waiting For: 2026–2030

Our sneak peek at the most promising cars, trucks, and SUVs of the next few years.

Even in the age of next-day delivery, self-checkout, and gigabit internet, some things can't be rushed. The cars, trucks, and SUVs seen here won't reach dealer lots for anywhere from a few months to a few years. Some of them are about to roll down the assembly line. Others haven't emerged from the design studio yet. We're telling you about them now, though, because these are the vehicles that will matter, regardless of how many boring crossovers automakers puke out. These are worth the wait.

The Alfa Romeo Stelvio is being thoroughly rethought for its second generation, which was supposed to arrive in 2026 but has now been delayed until 2027 at the earliest. While it will still sport Alfa Romeo's typically sensual styling, the SUV will now be sold with a choice of either a hybrid or a fully electric powertrain. The Stelvio will also migrate to the STLA Large platform, which could push the compact SUV closer to mid-size territory. A future performance-oriented Quadrifoglio variant could make use of the Hurricane twin-turbocharged inline-six that is also found in its platform-mate, the Dodge Charger.

Audi is planning a new electric sports car based on the radical Concept C. Positioned somewhere between the now-dead TT and R8 sports cars, the Concept C will usher in a new design language for the brand, with bold lighting, clean surfacing, and an interior centered around high-quality materials. The Audi will share its platform with the upcoming Porsche 718 EVs, and the electric sports car will likely launch with both a rear-wheel-drive single-motor setup and an all-wheel-drive dual-motor powertrain. We're expecting the TT successor to arrive at some point in 2027 with a price approaching $100,000.

BMW's venerable 3-series sports sedan is now complemented by an electric variant called the i3, which rides on the same new 800-volt architecture as the iX3 SUV. The i3 will also spawn the first proper electric M car, with the electric M3 expected to pack a potent quad-motor powertrain. The i3 goes on sale in the U.S. at the end of 2026, and we expect the electric M3 to follow in 2027.

Pickup trucks are big business in the United States, and Chevy is overhauling its moneymaker for 2027. The next-generation Silverado goes on sale by the end of 2026 with reworked styling that doesn't stray far from the current generation's assertive look. The big changes are under the skin, where the turbocharged four-cylinder and Duramax diesel are joined by two new small-block V-8s, one measuring 5.7 liters and the other at 6.6 liters. We're still waiting on power figures for the new V-8s, but they are expected to be more efficient than the engines they replace. The cabin also gets far more modern with a new 16.3-inch touchscreen and a 12.2-inch digital gauge cluster that are standard across the lineup.

The Chevy Camaro is set to make a triumphant return for the 2029 model year. The iconic pony car will likely return with two doors, but there's a strong chance that Chevy offers it in a four-door configuration too, since it will share a platform with new sedans from Buick and Cadillac. A turbocharged four-cylinder engine will likely be the base powertrain, while the Camaro is also expected to borrow the new 535-hp 6.7-liter V-8 from the Corvette. A 10-speed automatic will hopefully be joined by a six-speed manual. Production is expected to kick off in late 2028, and the starting price will probably be around $40,000.

Just as the Hemi V-8 returned to the Ram 1500 pickup truck, so too will the eight-cylinder squeeze its way back under the hood of the Dodge Charger. The electric Charger Daytona has failed to catch on, and the return of the V-8 should help the muscle car regain the adoration of the Dodge fanbase. The V-8 will likely be reintroduced in 5.7-liter, 6.4-liter, and Hellcat-badged supercharged 6.2-liter form, and power outputs should remain mostly the same, with the Hellcat easily topping 700 ponies. Look for the Hemi V-8 to reappear in the Charger sometime in 2027.

Dodge is gearing up to launch a new flagship sports car, but the Copperhead won't be a direct replacement for the beloved Viper. Instead of a slinky V-10-powered coupe, Dodge says the Copperhead will be a "hyper-muscle car." The dramatic styling will be draped over a coupe body that is smaller than the current Charger and covered with aerodynamic doodads. Under the hood, the Copperhead could feature a Hemi V-8, but Dodge has also suggested that global synergies with other brands under the Stellantis umbrella could play a role, perhaps opening the way for the use of Maserati's Nettuno V-6. Regardless, the Copperhead will likely be loud, powerful, and fast, with prices expected to eclipse $100,000 when it arrives in 2029.

The Ferrari Luce marks the start of a new era for the famous Italian automaker, which will sell its famed V-12 engines for as long as it can, but has also decided to cater to a different crowd with a high-performance EV. The low-slung four-door features a quad-motor powertrain spitting out a whopping 1035 horsepower, allowing the Luce to zip to 62 mph in a claimed 2.5 seconds. The 122-kWh battery should provide around 280 miles of range and can recharge at up to 350 kilowatts. The styling, penned in part by former Apple designer Jony Ive, has been divisive for its smooth shape and tall stance. Inside, the Luce mixes modern screens with traditional dials and buttons. The Luce will start at well over $600,000, and U.S. deliveries are expected to start in Q2 2027.

Despite discontinuing the F-150 Lightning EV, Ford isn't giving up on electric trucks. The Blue Oval is developing the new "Universal Electric Vehicle" platform, which will spawn a variety of vehicles, starting with a new compact electric truck called the Fathom. Roughly the size of the Maverick, the Fathom will have much more interior space thanks to its electric powertrain and will be simpler to build, with 20 percent fewer parts. Ford will use lithium-iron-phosphate batteries to keep costs down while still delivering around 300 miles of range, and Ford also says the truck will match a four-cylinder Mustang to 60 mph. Pricing will start at $29,945, with production expected to kick off in the second half of 2027.

Sure, Genesis already has a flagship sedan, but no self-respecting luxury brand can do without a top-dog crossover these days. Enter the GV90, a large three-row electric SUV with all the presence and size you expect from a range-topping model. It comes standard with a dual-motor, all-wheel-drive powertrain good for 657 horsepower and a 310-mile range. The real highlight, though, is the lavish interior and the available coach doors on the Neolun model. Sales start in early 2027, and we expect pricing to come in at around $150,000.

Genesis wants to prove it can do performance as well as luxury, and the electric GV60 Magma will be followed up by the Magma GT. Instead of electric motors, however, the slinky coupe will pack a mid-mounted twin-turbocharged V-8 engine that should produce well over 600 hp. The V-8 could also be joined by a V-6 hybrid powertrain, and the Magma GT will spawn a convertible model as well as a hardcore track-focused trim. Genesis plans to take the Magma GT racing, and production should start by late 2027.

Originally expected to wear a Lexus badge, the Toyota-developed supercar will actually arrive as the first standalone model under the GR performance brand. Called the GR GT, the aggressive bodywork is wrapped around a new aluminum structure. The engine bay packs a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8, hooked up to a mechanical limited-slip differential and an eight-speed transaxle, the latter of which also houses an electric motor. All told, the hybrid powertrain churns out 641 hp and 627 pound-feet of torque, providing a claimed top speed of 199 mph. Toyota says the curb weight is 3858 pounds. Prices are expected to start at around $300,000, and sales should start in late 2027.

Infiniti is going back to its roots with a new Q50 sports sedan for 2028. Playing off the popularity among enthusiasts of the G35 coupe of the early 2000s, the revived Q50 sedan will pack a twin-turbocharged V-6 engine borrowed from the Nissan Z and producing at least 400 horsepower. Better yet, Infiniti is strongly considering a manual transmission to make the Q50 even more engaging. The Q50 should return in 2027, and pricing should start at around $60,000.

Jaguar has thrown out the playbook and will start afresh in mid-2027 when production of the Type 01 gets underway. The large, four-door grand tourer will be the first model in a line of new EVs as Jaguar attempts to move upmarket to compete with the likes of Bentley. The Type 01 is boldly styled, taking its blocky front end and dramatic proportions from the Type 00 concept. Range is estimated at 400 miles, while the tri-motor powertrain churns out 1015 hp and 1007 pound-feet of torque. Pricing will start at around $130,500 as Jaguar aims to capture a wealthier, younger audience.

The iconic Wrangler will gain a new halo model with the Scrambler, a two-door pickup truck with a removable roof panel and retro styling. Previewed by a concept car shown at SEMA, the new front-end design is inspired by Kaiser Jeeps of the 1960s. Under the hood, we expect the Scrambler to pack the 392 Hemi 6.4-liter V-8, producing at least 470 hp and 470 pound-feet of torque. The Scrambler will also break from Wrangler tradition with an independent front suspension. The concept also featured unique setup with seats that could be mounted rearward in the bed, but we're unsure if this will make production. Prices will likely start over $90,000, and we expect the Wrangler Scrambler to arrive in 2028.

Lexus signaled its interest in a high-performance EV with the Electrified Sport concept in 2021 and doubled down with the LFA concept in 2025. The concept utilizes the same aluminum platform as the hybrid GR GT, but with an unspecified electric powertrain. Lexus had said the Electrified Sport would be capable of a 60 mph sprint in the low 2.0-second range and a range of over 430 miles thanks to solid-state batteries, but those figures could change by the time the new LFA launches in a few years. Lexus has also hinted at a simulated manual transmission in the past, which could help differentiate the LFA EV.

The Mazda CX-5 is the brand's bestselling model and will get a boost with the addition of a hybrid powertrain in 2027. Mazda already revealed the design of the new generation for the nonhybrid model, and it shares a similarly slick look to the outgoing CX-5. The standard 187-hp four-cylinder engine will be joined by a Mazda-developed hybrid powertrain for the 2027 model year, which is expected to make use of Mazda's 2.5-liter inline-four engine and should push the EPA-rated fuel economy over the 30-mpg mark.

Mitsubishi will re-enter the off-road SUV ring with a new Montero. While Mitsubishi is launching a new Pajero (historically rebadged as Montero for the U.S.) for other markets based on its own Triton pickup (pictured here), the U.S. market may end up getting an SUV based on a body-on-frame platform borrowed from Nissan. Although the Pajero uses a 2.4-liter turbo-diesel, the U.S.-bound Montero is expected to employ a twin-turbocharged V-6, and possibly offer a hybrid model as well. Prices should start in the low-$60,000 range, and the Montero may not go on sale till 2030.

Nissan is reviving the Xterra nameplate for a new off-road-focused SUV. Due out in 2028, the new Xterra will feature boxy bodywork and a body-on-frame platform for true all-terrain chops. The four-wheel-drive system is expected to be hooked up to a V-6 hybrid powertrain. Nissan is targeting a price point of around $40,000 for its new off-roader.

So far, Porsche's electric lineup includes the Taycan sedan and Macan EV SUV, but the brand's sports cars will begin to transition to battery power soon. The first entry will be the EV version of the 718 Boxster and Cayman mid-engine models, due in 2027. We're eagerly anticipating these cars because Porsche is promising lots of horsepower, the same balanced chassis as the gas versions, and even a dynamic soundtrack of some sort.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine. He has been part of the Hearst Autos team since 2016 and now lives in New York City.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

#4394. Rivian's New Robots Will Initially Handle 20% Of Factory Tasks. The Goal Is 80%, CEO Says

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian, the California-based startup that makes the R1S, R1T, and R2 EVs, wants to flood its car factories with robots. In an interview with Kleiner Perkins, RJ Scaringe, the company’s founder and CEO, said that as much as 80% of the assembly line tasks will be automated, and it’s all thanks to the Mind Robotics spinoff established last year.

We don’t know when the robot revolution will hit Rivian’s factory floors, but Scaringe said that things will start off at a smaller scale.

“In the beginning, we’re going to be able to do 20% of the tasks on the plant, but over time, we want to grow that to 80%,” said Scaringe. “And that’s what makes software so exciting and why designing the hardware with headroom is so important.”

To be clear, the vast majority of car plants in the world, including Rivian’s, have some degree of automation. We’ve all seen those huge robot arms that pick up various parts and install them in fixed positions. These robots are manually programmed to do the same task over and over again, and they can only do their job if the parts they need are exactly in the same spot every time.

However, what Rivian—and others like it—aims to do in the future is replace humans who do highly repetitive tasks that have some degree of variability. At first, posts where humans simply pick up a part from a bin and place it on a fixture will be handled by AI-enabled robots that are able to detect small variations in where parts are placed inside the bin.

“These are the immediate opportunities we see,” said Scaringe. “And these tend to be the ones that often are the least interesting jobs. But there’s a huge body of work that exists there. Depending on the section of the plant, up to 50% of the labor is in pick-and-place [posts].”

To make it all happen, Rivian has worked closely with Mind Robotics, a startup that the EV maker spun off last year to develop autonomous driving and “physical AI.” Now, RJ Scaringe revealed that both companies have poached talent from the consumer electronics industry to work on Rivian’s future software and hardware plans.

“We have a lot of folks, both within Rivian and Mind, that we’ve recruited from consumer electronics. Like, if you’re working on a tactile-sensing phone, how is that helpful on a robot? Well, a robot needs to have tactile sensing. So, there are these deep capabilities that have been built into the consumer electronics space that we’ve leveraged within Rivian, and we’re leveraging with Mind,” said Scaringe.

In practice, engineers filmed how various tasks are completed on the factory floor and then fed those videos into software that can decode what’s happening in each frame. Then, the software can issue commands to the robot.

“In the case of manufacturing, what we’ve done within Mind, we’ve taken videos of a whole broad spectrum of tasks. So, thousands of tasks being done, characterized what’s in those tasks, what’s the degree of difficulty from a dexterity point of view and a reasoning point of view,” said Rivian’s CEO. With the proper hardware in place, the software can then be improved over time. "The model gets smarter over time,” added Scaringe.

That’s similar to what the company aims to do with its Gen2 R1S and R1T electric models. The two EVs are equipped with all of the necessary hardware to enable point-to-point hands-free driving, while the software that ties it all together is scheduled to become available on a small scale through an over-the-air software update in late 2026, followed by a wider rollout in 2027.

#4393. Here's Every New Electric Vehicle Model for Sale in the U.S. for 2027

Range, efficiency, and base price: This guide will help you decide on the EV that works best for you.

Electric vehicles make up a small percentage of the total automotive market today, but their appeal continues to grow as the automakers expand their range, performance, and style—and as recharging becomes quicker and easier. Shoppers looking for zero-emissions driving now have an expansive list of vehicles to choose from, with a wide variety of body styles and several different price points. To make it easy on you, we've compiled them all in one place so you can choose the best EV that's right for your family, lifestyle, and driving habits. Please note that this list includes only those EVs that draw their power from the country's electrical power grid, which means it doesn’t include the few available fuel-cell cars that propel themselves with electricity but are fueled by hydrogen.

Think of the A6 e-tron as the electric equivalent to Audi's long-running gas-powered A6 sedan, pairing handsome, if reserved, styling with impressive range. There's also a sportier S6 e-tron variant that produces nearly 500 horsepower.

The e-tron GT is effectively a Porsche Taycan in Audi clothing. It's a quick and fun sports sedan that's neither particularly spacious nor inexpensive.

The Q4 e-tron is Audi's compact electric SUV, and shares components with the Volkswagen ID.4. The Q4 e-tron is offered as both a traditional SUV and as a Sportback model with a more coupe-like roofline.

The Audi Q6 e-tron is a compact electric luxury SUV that is around seven inches longer than the Q4 e-tron. Audi also offers the performance-focused SQ6 e-tron, which features a more potent dual-motor powertrain. Both the Q6 and SQ6 are offered as a Sportback variant with a sloping roofline.

BMW's electric equivalent to the gas- and gas-electric 5-series goes by the name i5, and it's arguably the better-driving mid-size BMW sedan option.

The i7 is the electric sister vehicle to BMW’s long-running flagship sedan, the 7-series, and shares its bold design with its gas-powered relative.

The BMW iX3 is a compact luxury SUV that is essentially the electric equivalent of the brand’s popular X3 gas-powered SUV. It is the first BMW EV to reach the U.S. riding on the company’s Neue Klasse platform.

The Cadillac Optiq is a compact electric luxury SUV that utilizes the same platform and powertrain as the Chevrolet Equinox EV, and is also offered with a performance-oriented V-series model.

Cadillac’s first entry into the luxury electric SUV category is the slick-looking Lyriq. It shares its battery tech with other high-profile GM EVs, including the GMC Hummer EV pickup truck, but it wears a more upscale wardrobe. The rear-wheel-drive model offers the most range. The all-wheel-drive model adds an additional electric motor to produce a combined 500 horsepower. Unlike Caddy’s sports sedans, the Lyriq’s driving demeanor takes on a more comfortable, cruising-focused feel, and the quiet cabin is spacious for both people and cargo.

The Cadillac Vistiq is a mid-size electric luxury SUV with three rows of seating, which slots in above the Lyriq and serves as an effective replacement for the gas-powered XT6.

The Cadillac Escalade IQ is a full-size luxury SUV that borrows the first part of its name from Cadillac's long-running gas-powered behemoth but features an electric powertrain under its bold bodywork. Cadillac also offers an IQL variant that is 4.2 inches longer, providing extra third-row legroom and cargo space.

The Celestiq is an ultra-luxurious behemoth, measuring over 18 feet long and packed with modern tech and rich materials. Each Celestiq is special-ordered, entirely bespoke, and incredibly expensive, with prices starting around $340,000.

The Bolt returns after a brief hiatus as Chevy's smallest and most affordable EV, starting at just $28,995.

The Chevrolet Equinox EV is a compact electric SUV that carries a starting price of just under $35,000.

Apart from being a midsize two-row Chevy SUV wearing aggressive styling, the Blazer EV shares little in common with its gas-powered relative. The Blazer EV comes in three trim levels: LT, RS, and SS. Many drivetrain combinations are available, ranging from a mild single-motor front-wheel-drive setup for the base LT to a wild 550-plus horsepower dual-motor all-wheel-drive fitment for the SS. Additionally, there are two lithium-ion battery packs to choose from. Range varies depending on battery and motor configuration.

Despite sharing its name with the conventionally powered Silverado truck, the Silverado EV is a clean-sheet design and is offered in a wide range of configurations, from a work truck to the high-powered 760-hp LT and the off-road-tuned Trail Boss.

The Dodge Charger Daytona is an electric muscle car and Dodge's first electric vehicle, available as both a two-door coupe and a four-door sedan.

The Fiat 500 hatchback returns to our shores for 2024. Except this time, it's an electric-only affair, as reflected by its 500e moniker. Though this little Fiat oozes style, its driving range is a bit disappointing. Though the EPA has yet to release an official estimate, Fiat is advertising an estimated 149-mile range from this sub-$40,000 city car.

Although legally considered a "Low Speed Vehicle," the Topolino can be converted to be road legal and provides a new entry point for the EV market with its $14,985 price tag. Just don't expect it to do all the same things a normal car can do, with a top speed of just 25 mph and a range of 46 miles.

It may not have two doors or a V-8, but the Ford Mustang Mach-E has the looks and driving dynamics to warrant its wearing of the Blue Oval's pony car nameplate.

#4392. 10 Pokémon Characters Who Deserved Much More Attention

Laurence Wall is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been writing professionally since 2022 and covering games since 2023. He primarily writes guides and lists, with a focus on indie games, RPGs, ARPGs, Soulslikes, MMOs, card games, boss fights, and detailed tutorials. Before joining DualShockers, Laurence worked as

While Pokémon is best known for the Pokémon themselves, every game brings an eclectic cast of characters we interact with as Pokémon trainers. Whether it’s quirky Gym Leaders, angsty rivals, or just odd folks you meet along the way, your journey is punctuated by these interesting experiences.

This list covers some of the best things players find when taking their time in the Pokémon series.

However, sometimes a character comes along that really makes you pay attention. Maybe it’s the way they look, what they said, or the Pokémon they used, but they stick in your memory somehow. The Pokémon series is full of these characters. More often than not, they appear and disappear as fast as they were introduced, leaving you a little confused about why they didn’t play a bigger role.

Here are a few examples of characters I wish had a bigger role, or were fleshed out a bit more over the course of all nine Generations to date.

Anyone who played the original Diamond and Pearl back in the day will remember Cheryl. She’s the helpful trainer who accompanies you through Eterna Forest, right before the second gym. You might think she doesn’t have much of a role, since all she does is heal your Pokémon with her Chansey and then wander off, yet she seems to recur throughout the franchise.

Cheryl reappears later in the Battleground, a place generally reserved for powerful trainers, with a team of Pokémon with crazy-high HP stats, and also in the Battle Tower. She also appears in Pokémon Generations, getting lost in The Old Chateau, and seems to have a relative in Hisui called Sabi.

It’s a shame we never got to see a bit more from Cheryl in the story, or even in something like Pokémon Contests!

Mohn has always been a pretty interesting character in Pokémon Sun and Moon. You’ll originally meet him when you’re introduced to the Poke Pelago; however, you might notice he looks a little familiar.

Long story short, Mohn was originally a researcher at the Aether Foundation and Lusamine's husband. However, when we meet him, he’s unfortunately lost his memory. It’s rumoured that when researching the Ultra Wormholes, he fell into one and developed amnesia, but this topic isn’t really explored much.

I would have loved a bit more backstory about Mohn, his relationship with his family and just what happened to him when travelling through Ultra Space. However, we may never know.

Marley, like Cheryl, is a Generation 4 character we meet while exploring a certain area of the game. This area is an offshoot of Victory Road and can only be explored in the Post-Game.

Marley doesn’t like to talk much and seems very caring. As such, while she does have an Arcanine, it’s also equipped with Helping Hand to assist you in battle. Like Cheryl, she can also be found in the Battleground and the Battle Tower, and she specialises in high-speed Pokémon.

The thing is, Marley obviously has a connection to Shaymin, which the game doesn’t really develop much. She helps us reach Seabreak Path and can even be found there again if you bring Oak’s Letter. On top of this, in Pokémon Masters, she even has a Shaymin! Is she just an interested trainer, or is there more to it?

Malva is the Fire-type Elite Four member of the Kalos region. Most Elite Four members don’t have much to offer, aside from an interesting design. However, Malva is hiding something far more sinister beneath the surface.

From Ultra Necrozma’s stat boosts to Volo’s grueling final battle, these Pokémon encounters bend the rules to deliver memorable challenges.

See, Malva is actually part of the heinous Team Flare, which you work to dismantle throughout the game. We learn later, in Legends Z-A, that Malva was there when they captured the legendary Pokémon Yveltal and helped take it down.

This is why she seems so prickly towards you when you face her in the Pokémon League. I would have liked to see a bit more of Malva and learn more about her involvement with Team Flare. The Flare storyline always seemed a bit weak after all.

Thankfully, Malva seems to learn her lesson and helps us with Dr Xerosic in the X and Y postgame, somewhat redeeming herself.

Benga is a really odd character. He’s obviously the Grandson of the Champion, Alder; that’s pretty obvious from his radical hairstyle. However, it’s never explained how Benga got so powerful. More so than his Grandfather, the Champion, might I repeat!

Benga is the final boss of the White Treehollow in White 2 or the Black Tower in Black 2. As such, he has an absolutely ludicrous team of Latios/Latias, Garchomp/Dragonite, and a Volcarona. While the Volcarona is obviously a nod to Alder, how on earth did this little kid get his hands on a pair of legendaries?

Once you’ve defeated him, you can head back to Floccesy Town, where Benga will offer you either a Shiny Gible or a Shiny Dratini. Now he seems to have shiny Pokémon to offer you, but how did he get these? This kid is a real mystery.

Starting in Generation 5, you can find Ingo in the Battle Subway, where he serves as a main boss alongside his brother Emmet. And for a long time, that’s where he stayed. A fairly obscure, relatively uninteresting character who didn’t draw much attention.

However, you might be surprised to come across Ingo in Hisui, in Pokémon Legends: Arceus. And no, this isn’t some ancient relative like most other Sinnoh trainers; this really is Ingo, having travelled through time and lost a good chunk of his memories. But why him, and not a Sinnoh character?

Thankfully, Ingo gets a happy ending, as we learn in Legends Z-A that he eventually returned to Unova and reunited with his brother Emmet. Turns out even the most unassuming trainer can have their secrets!

And speaking of people being zapped across Space and Time, here we have Anabel. We were originally introduced to Anabel in Pokémon Emerald, where she served as a Frontier Brain, one of the most powerful and difficult trainers in the entire series.

After defeating the Elite Four, these are the Pokémon Games Where the Post-Game Feels Like a Whole New Adventure.

However, fast-forward to Pokémon Sun and Moon, and we meet Anabel again; like Ingo, she’s been mysteriously transported to Alola, this time through an Ultra Wormhole rather than by Arceus. Now she’s part of the International Police, and as part of the UB task force, she’s there to round up the rabid Ultra Beasts rampaging across the region.

We know Anabel is a strong trainer, before and after the incident, but how did she enter the Ultra Wormhole in the first place? Was she chosen? Or was it just random chance? We never really get an answer here. It would have been nice to get a little more backstory into what happened in Hoenn.

Zinnia appears only in the Generation 3 remakes, Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire. During the adventure, you run into her masquerading as part of the evil team, but you soon learn she’s actually part of an ancient group trying to summon Rayquaza.

She plays a larger role in the Delta Episode; however, all her efforts are for nothing, as the main character ends up Mega Evolving Rayquaza and stopping the Meteor.

Zinnia has a fantastic, interesting design, and the bits and pieces we get of her backstory make it seem like she’ll play a bigger role in the story. She seems to know so much more than we do, especially about the Pokémon Multiverse, but again, we never fully explore her story. At least we still have that incredible battle theme!

If you’ve played Pokémon Colosseum or XD, you’ll have fond memories of this utterly bizarre trainer. Miror B is a funky villain and one of the four admins of Team Cipher. However, you’ll quickly notice that while he might be on the bad side, his real passion is actually dancing!

And not only does he like to bust a move, but his Pokémon do too! And, I have to admit, he’s got one of the best battle songs in the entire Pokémon series! The cool thing about Miror B is that, once defeated, he actually leaves Team Cipher in order to set up his own group, whom you meet in the sequel. He might never quite renounce his wicked ways, but for entertainment, you don’t get much better than this.

It’s certainly a shame we never got to see more of Miror B, as Game Freak seems determined to ignore Genius Sonority’s twin masterpieces.

Yep, this is one for the OGs. I remember back in Primary school, when rumours of Mew being under the truck were still floating around, there was another rumour about the dark side of the kind and generous Mr. Fuji.

The thing is, this one actually holds water, unlike the Mew story. You first find Mr. Fuji in Lavender Town, looking after orphaned Pokémon, and defending the Marowak from Team Rocket in Pokémon Tower. We later learn that Mr. Fuji and Blaine were good friends, and that they both worked on a project in the burned-down Pokémon Mansion over on Cinnabar.

Of course, the theory is that Mr. Fuji was one of the scientists who created Mewtwo through genetic experimentation on Mew. He was so traumatised by his creation that he vowed never to hurt a Pokémon again, and moved to Lavender Town to atone for his misdeeds.

This theory is reflected in the Pokémon Origins series and in Dr. Fuji in Mewtwo Strikes Back. We also know Mr. Fuji travelled to Faraway Island and left a note for the trainer before they find Mew. Was this the original Mew used to create Mewtwo?

However, I'm fairly certain we never actually got the official answer to this theory in the mainline games. For now, we’ll have to rely on theories to sate our appetite for Pokémon lore! Maybe one day we’ll know for sure?

From NPC placements to move typings, these are the Pokémon FireRed & LeafGreen Changes That Quietly Improved the Original Games.

#4390. Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

Unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The company publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.

It comes just four days after Elon Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.

UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”

In exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the company wrote.

UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.

And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP says it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.

The post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.

UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the company’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.

Musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He said Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”

If the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.

As we reported when Tesla announced the wind-down, that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.

The real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks, a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.

Even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, launched a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August. None of it fixed demand.

I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.

Of course, it’s more complicated than that.

There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.

First off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.

Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.

In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.

I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

No way Musk lets an outside third party find out how much it really costs to build these things.

You could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too big a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid.

If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the company to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.

But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

#4389. Every EV from Every Brand in America

We've created this handy guide to let you know all the brands that sell electric vehicles in the United States.

While gas-powered vehicles still make up an overwhelming majority of cars sold in the United States, their market share is slowly getting chipped away at by battery-electric ones. Since the Nissan Leaf and Tesla Roadster brought electric vehicles back to the national stage in the late 2000s, automakers have worked overtime to noticeably improve the charging speeds and driving ranges of their battery-powered products. No longer limited to small cars, EVs now take up space in just about every automotive segment.

We've compiled an exhaustive list of today's options to make it easy to determine what electric vehicles are available from which automotive brands in the United States. Don't go looking for hydrogen-powered electric vehicles here, though, as we've excluded those from this list.

Audi sells an array of electric SUVs and cars, from the compact Q4 e-tron to the range-topping 912-hp RS e-tron GT. Both of Audi's electric SUVs are available in either wagon or fastback body styles.

BMW's EV sedans look similar to their gas-powered cars, but the iX3 and incoming i3 promise next-generation looks and technology.

Cadillac's lineup of electric vehicles consists of an SUV in nearly every size, including the Escalade IQ, which looks just as ostentatious as the gas-powered Escalade despite its silent powertrain.

Chevrolet's electric vehicle arsenal is centered around SUVs, but the American automaker also caters to business owners with the WT version of the Silverado EV pickup truck.

Dodge currently sells just one EV, the Charger Daytona, which is available as either a coupe or sedan. It assumes the muscle car role vacated by the previous Scat Pack and Hellcat versions of the Charger and Challenger.

The only Fiat sold in the United States right now is an electric version of the company's iconic 500 city car. Fiat also offers the Topolino, which is technically classified as a "Low Speed Vehicle" and is limited to 25 mph.

Ford sells two electric models, the Mustang Mach-E SUV and the E-Transit commercial van.

The Genesis Electrified GV70 is based on the Korean automaker's popular compact SUV, while the GV60 utilizes the same platform found under the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6.

GMC's lineup of electric vehicles is just as big and brash as its gas-powered offerings. Two pickups and an SUV are available.

Hyundai has won Car and Driver's EV of the Year award three times in a row, first with the Ioniq 5 SUV in 2022 and then with the Ioniq 6 sedan in 2023. The high-powered Ioniq 5 N, which entertains with faux gearshifts and engine noises, won the award in 2024.

Jeep currently sells two EVs in the U.S. Although the Wagoneer S shares the first part of its name with the gas-powered Wagoneer, the EV is completely unrelated to that behemoth. The Recon is an electric alternative to the off-road-ready Wrangler.

Kia's lineup of EVs currently consists of a trio of SUVs.

Lexus currently sells two EVs in the United States: the RZ SUV, which is related to the Toyota bZ, and an electric version of the ES sedan.

California-based startup Lucid Motors exclusively builds EVs and recently launched its second model, the Gravity SUV.

The Italian luxury brand currently offers three EVs in the U.S., all of which are related to the brand's gas-powered models and carry the Folgore suffix to distinguish them as battery-powered.

Mercedes offers a vast range of EVs, from sedans to SUVs and even vans. The automaker has begun shifting away from its "EQ" naming structure for EVs, starting with the electric G-class, which dons the name G580 with EQ Technology. It's a wordy solution that'll also appear on the upcoming battery-electric 2026 CLA-class.

While Mini previously sold an electric variation of its iconic Cooper hatchback, the latest version has been delayed indefinitely, meaning Mini currently offers just one EV in the U.S., a battery-powered variant of its Countryman SUV

Nissan sells one EV in the United States, the Leaf, which has transformed from a hatchback to an SUV for its third generation.

There are currently three Porsche EVs on sale in the U.S., with an electric successor to its 718 sports car on the way.

Ram, the truck division spun off from Dodge in 2009, currently sells one EV. Ram had originally aimed to start building the 1500 REV in late 2024 for deliveries in early 2025, but the electric pickup truck is now delayed to late 2026.
